Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs389.28 per litre while HSD will cost Rs412.12 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will be applicable for Sept 25 (Friday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Xi sets red lines for Trump despite lavish White House welcome. Chinese President Xi Jinping told his US counterpart, Donald Trump, on Thursday that Beijing and Washington must peacefully manage their superpower rivalry, as the US president gave his Chinese counterpart a lavish welcome to the White House. While Trump hailed their “truly great friendship” on a day of sweeping pomp and circumstance, Xi used his state visit to lay down China’s red lines on AI, Taiwan and the war on Iran. Behind the pageantry — and symbolic gestures like Trump taking Xi inside his Marine One helicopter — the talks were focused on tensions that continue to divide the world’s two largest economies. In his opening remarks with Trump, Xi said the two countries must ensure there is “no conflict and no confrontation between us”. Xi also warned that the development of artificial intelligence should be “always under human control” — in contrast to Trump, who has repeatedly dismissed warnings that AI could threaten humanity itself. Trump’s remarks struck a warmer tone, underscoring the US president’s long-term efforts to woo the Chinese leader. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” Trump said after greeting Xi for his first visit to the White House in over a decade. The 80-year-old Trump said that the pair would “discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and super intelligence – SI,” his name for artificial intelligence. ‘Prudence’ But later as they met in the Oval Office, Xi urged Trump to show “prudence” and oppose independence for the flashpoint of Taiwan. The Chinese leader also urged Trump to end the war on Iran “through negotiation as soon as possible.” Few breakthroughs are expected during Xi’s state visit. Instead the trip is more about the spectacle as the world’s two biggest economies seek manage points of friction. A formal welcome on the White House South Lawn launched Thursday’s events, before Trump and Xi inspected a military parade on the newly paved-over Rose Garden. American military jets — including a B-2 bomber of the type that bombed Iranian nuclear facilities last year — then staged a flyover as US and Chinese flags flew over the West Wing. In the Oval Office, Trump joked that the Chinese had the friendliest press corps. His comment came days after he barred outlets CNN , MS Now and Politico from the White House — although they returned on Thursday after a court order. Trump later walked Xi out to see the new helipad he has built at the White House, and took the Chinese leader aboard his helicopter — one of the most exclusive and sensitive pieces of US military equipment. ‘Great meeting’ “We had a great meeting,” Trump said, as the pair ignored questions on subjects including Iran, Taiwan, fentanyl trafficking and jailed Hong Kong pro-democracy media mogul Jimmy Lai. Trump added that Xi was an “expert on stone aside from many other things and he loves good granite,” referring to the material used for the helipad, which he has boasted will last a million years. Trump will later throw a state dinner for Xi attended by top US tech CEOs. The menu features yellow squash veloute, sesame crusted sea bass, and vanilla cremeux with White House honey ice cream, the White House said. The charm offensive began Wednesday as Trump personally greeted Xi at the airport — the first time in more than six decades that a US president welcomed a foreign head of state in person at Joint Base Andrews near Washington. Trump said that the 73-year-old Xi looked “strong, vibrant, and fit,” following recent rumors about the Chinese leader’s health. But the flattery masked tensions over thorny topics including the trade war between the world’s top two economies sparked by Trump’s tariffs. In a small sign of progress, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Wednesday announced a two-month extension of a trade truce that was due to expire in November.

Authorities impose Section 144 in Karachi, ban gatherings of more than 5 people till Sept 30. KARACHI: Karachi joined other cities that have been put under Section 144 on Thursday as authorities imposed a ban on the gathering of more than five people in the city till Sept 30. The ban was notified in a Sept 24 order by Karachi Commissioner Hassan Naqvi. The notification, seen by Dawn , cited letters by the police. The letters reported “that protests, demonstrations, sit-ins and rallies are being held on major roads, junctions and roundabouts, causing severe traffic congestion and posing serious security concerns. Such road blockages are disrupting routine public life, impeding the movement of emergency services and restricting access to hospitals”, according to the notification. “There is reasonable apprehension that the holding, organising or facilitating of such gatherings, rallies, protests, demonstrations, processions and assemblies may obstruct public roads and thoroughfares, disrupt normal civic and commercial activities, cause inconvenience to the general public and traffic congestion, impede access to hospitals, and result in untoward incidents and deterioration of the law-and-order situation,” it said. It was, therefore, considered “necessary and expedient to impose preventive restrictions for a specified period to avert any possible untoward incident, maintain public peace and tranquility, safeguard the lives and property of citizens, ensure public safety and security, and facilitate the uninterrupted movement of the general public and essential services”, the notification said. It added that Section 144 was being implemented in the city, with a restriction on holding, organising, convening, facilitating or participating in any protest, demonstration, sit-in, rally, procession or other public gathering involving more than five people from Sept 24-30. The restriction has also been imposed in Sukkur and Hyderabad till Sept 29. Similar measures have been imposed elsewhere in the country ahead of PTI’s Sept 27 protest. Punjab has already imposed a ban on gatherings across the province for 13 days and prohibited inciting people to “unlawful assembly”. A similar ban under Section 144 has been enforced in Islamabad as well for two months. Gatherings in the federal capital are also banned under the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act 2024 , which had been rushed through the National Assembly amidst the opposition’s outcry ahead of a PTI gathering . The Balochistan government has also imposed Section 144 throughout the province for a 30-day period, citing reports indicating the likelihood of activities and gatherings that may adversely affect law and order and safety and security of the public.

SC rejects DHA plea for income tax exemption. ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court has dismissed four civil appeals filed by the Defence Housing Authority (DHA), Islamabad, against the denial of income tax exemption under Section 49 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, ruling that DHA is not a “local authority” for the purpose. A three-member bench headed by Chief Justice Yahya Afridi and comprising Justice Naeem Akhter Afghan and Justice Muhammad Shafi Siddiqui upheld the Islamabad High Court’s Jan 14, 2019, judgement, which had answered the tax references against DHA. Justice Siddiqui authored the judgement. The appeals arose from tax references filed in 2012. DHA had filed returns for tax years 2005 to 2008, claiming exemption under Section 49(2) on the ground that it was a local authority. The returns were treated as assessment orders under Section 120. Later, the Commissioner (Audit-II), LTU Islamabad, amended the assessments for 2005 to 2007, while the Additional Commissioner (Audit-II) amended the assessment for 2008 under Section 122(5A), treating them as erroneous and prejudicial to revenue on the ground that DHA did not fall within the expression “local authority”. Before the Supreme Court, Syed Tanseer Tassaduq Bukhari argued that DHA was a statutory authority responsible for the development, planning, regulation and administration of its area, exercised public and local powers, and that the expression “local authority” should not be construed narrowly. The Commissioner Inland Revenue (Zone-II), LTU Islamabad, represented by ASC Rehan Seerat and AOR Tariq Aziz supported the high court judgement and argued that DHA lacked the essential legal attributes of a local authority. Justice Siddiqui observed that the question was not whether DHA performed public or municipal functions within a defined area, but whether the nature and extent of its statutory powers satisfied the legal attributes of a “local authority” under Section 49(2).The court held that DHA’s case did not go beyond showing that it operated within a defined area and performed development, planning, regulation and administrative functions. The court subsequently held that DHA was not entitled to the exemption. Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

PTI ‘still in two minds’ over march plans to Islamabad. • Panjutha hints at possibility of postponement, links it to acceptance of party’s demands for Imran’s release, snap polls, probe into May 9 events • PTI spox says no such proposal being discussed, insists only founder can postpone march • Govt deploys Rangers in Islamabad, multiple districts of Punjab ahead of PTI protest ISLAMABAD: A PTI leader on Thursday hinted at the possibility of postponing its protest march if the federal government agreed to hold elections within six to eight months, release party chief Imran Khan and other political prisoners, and investigate May 9 and November 26 crackdowns on the opposition party. Advocate Naeem Haider Panjutha told Dawn that the protest could be postponed if these three assurances were given by the government. There was no clarity on where such a proposal originated from, which added to confusion about the PTI’s plans for its Sept 27 protest . Party spokesperson Sheikh Waqas Akram, however, denied any such proposal was being discussed at any party forum, saying only Imran Khan could take a decision even if such a proposal was on the table. “The first and primary condition is that the public mandate be respected and for that free, fair and tran­s­parent elections must be held within six to eight months,” Mr Panj­utha said, while demanding a clear guarantee that elections would be held before the end of this financial year. All political prisoners, including Imran Khan, must be released — not through any deal or political settlement, but through the courts and due process of law, he said, adding that all cases against Imran Khan were “weak”. The third demand was for a judicial inquiry into the events of May 9 and November 26. “If these three demands are fulfilled, the march can be postponed,” he said, adding that in case these demands were ignored, the PTI would be “coming with no compromise, no retreat, and no turning back”. On the other hand, Sheikh Waqas Akram told Dawn the above mentioned conditions were shared with the government after the D-Chowk incident, but the government had not responded positively, so the conditions were then withdrawn on the order of Imran Khan. “We have not received any concrete offer from the government side, so the long march will be held come what may. Even if we get an offer, we will demand to arrange a meeting with Imran Khan, as only he can postpone it,” he added. Sheikh Waqas said the PTI cannot afford to announce postponement of march, especially when its ministers were being abducted. In a meeting held at the opposition chamber in the Senate, PTI interim chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan and former senator Mustafa Nawaz Khokhar met Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas and discussed preparations for the planned long march. According to a statement issued by the Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayeen-i-Paki­stan (TTAP), the participants held a detailed discussion on the prevailing situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and growing challenges to provincial autonomy. The meeting also focused on the Sept 27 march, preparations for the event and the strategy to be adopted in the coming days. Rangers deployed Separately, the federal government approved the deployment of Rangers in Islamabad and several districts of Punjab from Sept 20 to Oct 5. “Pursuant to the request made by the chief commissioner, Islamabad Capital Territory … and Home Department, government of Punjab …, the federal government is pleased to authorise deployment of sufficient strength of troops of Pakistan Rangers (Punjab) in ICT and different districts of Punjab province,” an interior ministry notification read. The deployment has been aut­h­orised under Sections 7(b) and 10 of the Pakistan Rangers Ordin­ance, 1959, and Sections 4 and 5 of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, to perform functions specified under the laws, as authorised by the Islamabad chief commissioner or the provincial government. “The deployed troops may respond appropriately in self-defence to any threats or violent activities encountered in the course of their duties as per rules/regulations in vogue,” the notification stated. The Punjab government also sent a letter to the interior ministry requesting mobile and internet services at specific locations in Rawalpindi and Attock to be downgraded or jam­med on Sept 27. ‘Washington, Tehran exploring phased way out of war’. • Reports suggest Tehran could reopen Hormuz, may drop toll demand for blockade relief; but ‘neither side wants to move first’ • Gulf states press Trump for post-midterms war strategy; 80 countries call for full restoration of Gulf shipping • UAE bars Iranian airline flights WASHINGTON: US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to the talks said. The strait , through which a fifth of the world’s oil passes, has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the war. Iran wants relief from a blockade that is strangling its economy; Washington wants free passage restored for ships on the vital oil route that Tehran has kept closed. Talks are complicated by a familiar diplomatic problem: neither side wants to move first. Two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomats said the most workable option now on the table was a staged arrangement — Iran allowing ships through Hormuz in return for an end to the blockade and, potentially, access to frozen assets. “One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz,” a senior Iranian official said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Such a deal would require Donald Trump to accept another interim arrangement, after a previous understanding collapsed in July. The US president has suggested a fuller agreement might only be reached after November’s midterm elections. A senior European official said Iranian negotiators arrived in New York “with a very long list of demands”. The White House, for its part, has shown little urgency. “Iran is desperate for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States,” a White House official said, adding that “crushing sanctions” and “one of the most successful blockades in history” had left Tehran “completely broke”. Trump, the official suggested, was content to let an “inevitable Iranian collapse” continue rather than be rushed into concessions. Dennis Ross, a former US negotiator, put the chances of a deal before the midterms at roughly 30 per cent, though he noted both sides had reasons to want an agreement sooner rather than later. “The blockade is what’s really squeezing the Iranians. It’s strangling them,” he said. A pre-election deal could suit Trump too, easing Gulf tensions and helping bring down petrol prices at home. After the vote, Ross said, the president may feel freer to escalate pressure or consider military options. Tehran, meanwhile, is hedging. Even as it explores a diplomatic exit, Iran is preparing for the possibility of renewed conflict, accusing Washington of using the blockade and the threat of force as instruments of coercion. “Our fingers are on the trigger,” the senior Iranian official said. “The Americans know what they need to do but, because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this are extremely low.” Regional sources said Iran was prepared to drop, or at least set aside, its demand for transit fees on shipping through Hormuz in order to prioritise ending the blockade. “Iran is not primarily focused on imposing tolls in Hormuz but on preserving its administrative control of the waterway,” the senior official said. “Iran may be willing to defer the toll issue, but they are not going to give up administrative control of the strait.” At the heart of the diplomacy in New York is a fundamental tension. Washington wants pressure to produce concessions, Tehran wants pressure removed before making them, and the Gulf states want the conflict resolved without allowing the region’s strategic waterways to become enduring bargaining chips. In a separate meeting in New York, Gulf leaders pressed Trump for clarity on his strategy beyond the midterms, including whether Washington would resume military action if Iran refused to negotiate. They made clear their rejection of any Iranian control over Hormuz, insisting freedom of navigation be restored and that the strait must not become a tool of coercion — while also urging de-escalation, reflecting Gulf states’ desire to stay out of further confrontation. “It’s still not clear what Trump’s endgame is, or what the alternative to the pressure campaign would be,” said Ebtessam al-Ketbi, president of the Emirates Policy Center in Abu Dhabi. “The Iranians, by contrast, know what they want. They’re reshaping the regional landscape through Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb with a clear objective, while Washington has yet to define its roadmap.” Alan Eyre, another former US negotiator, warned that the blockade’s pressure could backfire: rather than softening its position, he said, Tehran was more likely to escalate, believing that any sign of weakness would prove fatal to the regime. Adding to the diplomatic pressure, a coalition of 80 countries called at the UN on Thursday for the full restoration of maritime navigation in the Gulf. “We call for the full restoration of navigational rights and principles without delay,” said Bahrain’s Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid al-Zayani, reading a joint statement to journalists. UAE suspends Iranian airline flights In a further sign of tightening pressure, the United Arab Emirates announced on Thursday that it would no longer accept flights operated by Iranian carriers, aligning itself with US sanctions targeting Iran’s aviation sector. Dubai has long been a key destination for Iranian airlines, serving multiple daily flights and a large Iranian community with close business ties to the emirate. The UAE’s General Civil Aviation Authority said the suspension was “based on the US sanctions imposed on Iranian airlines preventing them from using airports around the world”. The UAE, which was hit by thousands of Iranian missiles and drones early in the war, suspended trade and financial exchanges with Iran last month. On Wednesday its central bank blocked transactions with Iran’s Bank Melli, citing breaches of money-laundering, terrorism-financing and arms-proliferation rules. One passenger told AFP an Iran Airtour flight from Tehran to Dubai was cancelled shortly before departure on Thursday, after tickets had already been issued. Washington imposed sanctions on Iran’s aviation sector in early September, giving airlines until Wednesday to comply — including by halting the refuelling of Iranian aircraft — or risk being cut off from the dollar-based financial system. Iran’s main carriers were forced to cancel international flights this week as neighbouring states adopted similar restrictions; Turkmenistan turned back a flight from Tehran to Dushanbe on Thursday, an Iranian aviation official said, because it had not authorised the airline to fly. A handful of smaller Iranian carriers continue to operate abroad, notably to Armenia and to China, which has declined to follow Washington’s sanctions. Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

Govt working on 174 IMF-sought tweaks, NA panel told. • Proposed changes to be placed before parliament for approval • IMF mission to begin its review on 28th; Kristalina praises Pakistan’s performance in meeting with PM Shehbaz • Sovereign Wealth Fund, remittances, sugar policy among areas under discussion ISLAMABAD: The government on Thursday said the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was seeking about 174 amendments to various laws to improve governance in the financial sector, state-owned enterprises, foreign remittances, climate change and local currency integration as part of its two ongoing programmes worth $8.4 billion. “There are a total of 174 amendments the IMF wants to be passed,” Finance Secretary Imdadullah Bosal told the National Assembly Standing Committee on Finance and Revenue, presided over by Syed Naveed Qamar. He said the government was working on the amendments, which would be placed before parliament for approval. The statement came ahead of formal negotiations with a visiting IMF staff mission for the fourth review of the $7bn Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and the third review of the Resilience Support Facility (RSF), beginning on Monday. A day earlier, IMF Mana­ging Director Kristalina Geor­gieva — who met PM Shehbaz Sharif on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly — appreciated the country’s performance under its programme and praised the government’s efforts for economic stabilisation, which she noted were yielding tangible results. Mr Bosal said changes to the Sovereign Wealth Fund (SWF) law were also part of the discussions. He said the IMF had been clearly told that the proposed amendments would be presented to parliament, but their approval remained parliament’s prerogative. The SWF, covering five maj­or blue-chip companies, incl­u­ding OGDCL and Pakistan State Oil, has been a critical debating point of discussion as the IMF wants their governance and financial reporting standards to be brought at par with those applicable to other state-owned enterprises. The SWF group was created as a prospective investment vehicle for government-owned entities from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE, but little progress has been made. Mr Bosal said the government was also holding discussions with the IMF on remittances, which were critical to Pakistan’s external stability. He said efforts were needed to address costly payment-system impediments, while the IMF had strongly opposed subsidies for facilitating remi­ttances. Such subsidies, which had previously crossed Rs120bn, have already been withdrawn. He said changes to the sugar policy were also among the benchmarks for the IMF review and that the federal government had circulated a draft policy for liberalisation. Three provinces had agreed to the policy, while one had raised reservations that needed to be addressed. Committee Chairman Nav­eed Qamar questioned the government’s strategy for power distribution companies (Dis­cos), particularly the fate of loss-making entities. “You will give away the profitable Dis­cos, but what will happen to the remaining ones?” he asked. The panel stressed that economic reforms should be underpinned by a coherent, transparent and sustainable strategy, particularly where their implementation could impose additional costs on consumers, businesses and productive sectors of the economy. Mr Qamar said fiscal consolidation should be accompanied by measures to promote investment, exports, employment and sustainable economic growth. Members emphasised that assessment of the IMF programme should not remain confined to formal compliance with prescribed benchmarks but should also determine whether reforms were translating into measurable economic and social outcomes. The committee sought clearer information on implementation timelines, outstanding commitments, effectiveness of public expenditure and the implications of various reforms for citizens, businesses and taxpayers. The finance secretary reported that approximately $4.5bn had been disbursed by the IMF and three programme reviews had been completed. He said the programmes were supporting balance-of-payments needs and macroeconomic stability while requiring reforms relating to revenue mobilisation, debt sustainability, fiscal consolidation, taxation, the energy sector, SOE governance and trade liberalisation. The committee was informed that key programme commitments included parliamentary consideration of supplementary expenditure beyond approved budgets, restrictions on new tax amnesties and preferential tax treatment, energy-sector reforms and implementation of the National Fiscal Pact with the provinces. The panel also examined the retailer tax-registration scheme, with members questioning its limited initial participation and seeking a measurable assessment of its effectiveness. The committee called for an evaluation covering the number of registrations, revenue generated, compliance outcomes and whether the scheme’s existing design required further adjustment. It stressed that the finance ministry should assess the scheme’s performance over a defined period and hold implementing authorities accountable against clearly stated objectives. Members also sought detailed data on industrial captive-power users that had shifted to the national grid and asked for clarification about the implications for gas and petroleum consumption and circular debt. They said implementation of energy-sector reforms should be assessed against actual operational, financial and economic outcomes. The committee also reviewed the governance framework for state-owned enterprises and the reporting relationship between government-owned entities, their respective line ministries and the finance division. Officials said reporting lines had been clarified and proposed amendments were aimed at strengthening boards, improving governance and enhancing investment discipline within the Sovereign Wealth Fund framework. Situationer: Déjà vu at D-Chowk?. KHYBER Pakhtunkhwa is on edge again, and not just for the deteriorating security and volatility in the south, which has been bad for quite some time now. It is the provincial government’s avowed single-point agenda to secure its party’s chairman’s freedom from Adiala jail, or at the very least, get him some relief like shifting him to a private hospital in Islamabad. But days before ‘D-Day’, i.e. Sept 27, one cannot help but be struck by an overwhelming sense of déjà vu: this is November 2024 all over again, albeit with some changes to the cast. Ali Amin Gandapur, the chief minister at the time, who led the long march to D-Chowk, lost the job during his second year in office, allowing a young and relatively inexperienced Sohail Afr­idi to take up the mantle . One year into his term, the 37-year-old CM Afridi is now playing his biggest political gambit since his foray into politics as a student activist of the PTI’s student wing. There is another change to the cast. Bushra Bibi, the former first lady who led the bloody Nov 24 D-Chowk March, is now serving a jail term in Adiala jail. And so, the task of securing Imran Khan’s release has passed on to another woman — his sister, Aleema Khan. She too, though, has now been taken into custody . With the planned political onslaught on the federal capital just two days away, the clock is ticking, and worryingly, no one knows where and how this will end. No one has a clue. Not even those who have planned for this day for months. And neither do the ones who have scrambled to throw in all possible measures to defend and protect Islamabad from yet another onslaught from KP. The stakes are high and everyone with an insight knows it. The comparisons between the two guards are natural; Ali Amin was an old hack. He knew what he was getting into and would war-game it. But even he couldn’t forestall a mob that crossed over into the so-called Red Zone, precipitating violence in a way that was not foreseen. But Afridi is a relatively new campaigner, carrying the relentless pressure of the party’s D-Chowk fiasco. It seems he doesn’t know the full breadth of what he is getting into. These are uncharted waters for him and he doesn’t have the comfort of many wise counsels. Even the party’s own decision-making system is so diffused that no one is willing to publicly take responsibility for any fallout of the impending march; everyone is looking towards each other. Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Raja Nasir Abbas, the PTI’s current political mentors, are there to lend their support. But any decision, they have made clear, has to come from the PTI itself. Up until now, no one person knows what the whole plan is. With a crackdown on its leaders and lawmakers underway and authorities in Islamabad putting up several layers of security around the federal capital amid ominous warnings of nasty things to come, the PTI leadership can be under no illusions; this time around would be a different and dangerous gambit. There are logistical and financial issues as well. A party which had no dearth of resources finds itself struggling to raise money to mobilise its workers and pay for logistics. Adding to their woes is the unwillingness of private transporters to ferry party supporters, after having suffered huge losses to their vehicles in the Nov 2024 fiasco. So, what could be the game plan once party workers and supporters are eventually mobilised despite all the difficulties and misgivings? Stop at Swabi, just short of KP’s boundary with the Punjab on the M1 Motorway, and block the many entry points into Punjab? Stage a sit-in; but for how long? Will it be sustainable? Not just logistically but also politically, given the problems that the blockades would cause to the people, and the food and fuel shortages that these would give rise to? Or, will the PTI surge ahead, removing all the hurdles and battling police and Rangers to find an opening to enter Islamabad and bring the federal government to its knees, forcing it to accept their demands? If that is the case, then who will lead the charge? Who will take responsibility in the event of something going terribly wrong? It doesn’t take long for a seemingly well-organised ral­ly to turn into a mob; after all, even Ali Amin had not foreseen what would happen when his party workers entered the Red Zone. The risks are too high and everyone knows it — most of all the minders in Islamabad. PTI leaders now say, they are showing signs of panic by barricading their territory, placing containers and digging up roads to make them impassable. For the federal authorities, the risk of mob violence is too real to ignore. The events of Nov 2024 are still fresh in their memory and they can’t afford ano­ther violent confrontation so close to the Red Zone. Allowing the PTI to stage a sit-in anywhere near Islamabad is a big no-no for them; it was tried and tested, and it failed. The choices are limited. The PTI cannot afford a repeat of what happened in November 2024. Such an eventuality, they know, will hurt them gravely and might even cost them their government in KP. It is a suspense thriller, that’s for sure. No one kno­ws, neither in Peshawar, nor in Islamabad, how eve­nts will unfold in the days to come. Most worryingly, though, no one is talking to anyone, and no one knows who will initiate negotiations to end this deadlock. For some strange reason, in the words of a senior PTI lawmaker, they are looking to divine intervention to toss up some middle ground, or face-saving. Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

Dystopia, Inc: Would you like your news with or without hallucinations?. THE obituaries of news agencies have been written on many occasions over the past two decades. First we were told we were slower than Twitter and that our global network of salaried journalists was redundant because every citizen was a journalist now. Who needs to pay for ethically-produced fact-checked content when information from the source is flowing directly into our phones in real time? We all remember the euphoria of the Twitter Revolution in Iran in 2009 and the Facebook follow-up Arab Spring (2010-2012). It was intoxicating to see the free flow of information on social networks from citizens on the front line. THE obituaries of news agencies have been written on many occasions over the past two decades. But we also all remember the brutal comedown. What happens when the autocrats shut down the internet or throw your citizens in jail? Who continues to document the story in Iran or Egypt or Syria for the outside world? It turned out social media algorithms were not driven by a need to search for the truth. Silicon Valley worked out it would make more money promoting anger and outrage. It also turned out bad actors could manipulate these algorithms to promote lies. Not surprisingly, untrained citizens were not equipped to help society navigate the pollution of our information ecosystem. Wind forward another decade and we are here again as we are presented with another ‘news agency killer’, the utopian future of Artificial Intelligence. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Grok can scan the world’s journalism output in seconds and spit out five juicy paragraphs to tell you about anything that’s going on in the world. This is the so-called AI Overview — it is causing traffic to trusted journalism sites across the globe to crash and it rarely pays for the expensively-produced professional journalism it hoovers up. And so again we are asked: why pay for your professional journalism when information is being deli­vered free in real time? Why waste money employing journalists to ga­­ther information that can be aggregated by our new chatbot friends? Part of the answer lies in the little chatbot disclaimer which says the information in your AI overview may actually be wrong. Would you like your news with or without hallucinations? Getting to the facts costs money, time, expertise and effort. When a huge glacial collapse in late August triggered devastating flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border leaving more than 1,300 people dead, AFP deployed a team of 11 journalists on the ground in remote parts of Nepal and India. Within an hour of police confirmation of the first major flooding three of our journalists based in Kathmandu were on the road. Prakash Mathema, Anup Ojha and Prabin Ranabhat are all Nepalese. They know the language, the terrain and the people. They carried expensive cameras and drone equipment. One of our photographers made a 13-hour journey by motorbike and truck to reach the main disaster zone. He was then able to use his contacts to take an aid helicopter further into the disaster zone. His stunning drone images of destroyed villages were seen across the world. In a catastrophe in remote areas of the planet, often there is no internet. It requires journalists to be on the ground, sometimes putting themselves in considerable personal danger, to bear witness to events. It also requires journalists who know the country and can turn to a reliable source network. While part of our Nepal team headed to the mountains, the rest remained in Kathmandu to sift fact from rumour as stories of dead and missing emerged. Many of the first reliable words and pictures published by the global media came from agencies such as AFP and our colleagues at Reuters and AP . Our clients use the content without hesitation because they know it has been gathered in an ethically correct way according to the transparent charters and trust principles which guide the work of all our journalists. They know that we have emp­lo­yed professional journalists to ga­­ther information and that we invest resources in training and expertise to ensure the people we send into harm’s way are well prepared. Clients pay for the product bec­ause they understand quality news-gathering is not cheap. They also understand we work to the same ethical guidelines from every dateline on the planet. It makes no difference whether the content comes from Nepal or New York or Gaza, it bears the same stamp of quality. On the other hand, making stuff up costs nothing. Side by side with real journalistic images from the Nepal disaster zone were reams of deep fake images showing artificially generated destroyed villages and bodies lined up for burial. The tools that have given us AI Overviews have also given every human on the planet the capacity to create confusing and damaging false images that clog up our news feeds and often go viral on social media. At AFP we employ over 100 journalists exclusively working to debunk and fact check this growing fake tide. Pushing back on lies and manipulation has become an essential journalistic complement to searching for the truth. Defending truth and facts costs money and requires values. The international agencies’ global networks remain an essential part of the fabric of the global information system. They should be cherished, and defended. The writer is Global News Director at Agence France Presse (AFP). This opinion piece was commissioned as part of the World News Day campaign — which falls on Sept 27 — highlighting the essential role of journalism in providing facts and clarity. Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

Govt limits public disclosure of bureaucrats’ assets. • Selected asset information of BS-17, above officers to be made public • Government cites security concerns for withholding full asset declarations ISLAMABAD: The government will not fully disclose the assets of civil servants due to security concerns and will instead publish selected information by December this year to meet requirem­ents of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Finance Secretary Imdadullah Bosal told the National Assembly Stan­ding Committee on Finance and Revenue on Thursday. However, parliamentarians questioned why full details would not be made public when politicians, including the president and prime minister, were required to disclose their assets. They questioned why public servants should be treated differently when parliamentarians and politicians were required to make full asset declarations. Mr Bosal did not directly respond to the objection but said a lot of technical work had been undertaken by the Establishment Division and the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR). Under the mechanism, the FBR would assess the data and report its findings to the Establishment Division, which would have the power to initiate disciplinary action in case of any discrepancy. The fi­­nance secretary said civil servants’ asse­­ts would be declared under prescribed gui­delines but would not be published in full. The government has already moved to digitise declarations of income and assets of all federal civil servants in BS-17 and above, replacing the existing manual submission process with a dedicated FBR online portal. The declarations will undergo risk-based verification, while selected non-sensitive information will be made public. Soon afterwards, the Ministry of Fin­a­nce published on its website an office me­­morandum issued by the Establishment Division last week regarding the “digitisation of declaration of assets under Section 15-A of the Civil Servants Act, 1973”. According to the memorandum, the Establishment Division, in collaboration with the FBR, has launched a digitised system for the submission, verification and publication of declarations of income and assets under Section 15-A of the Civil Servants Act, 1973, and Rule 12 of the Civil Servants (Conduct) Rules, 2026. All officers in BS-17 and above are required to submit their declarations of income and assets for financial year 2025-26 through the dedicated FBR portal instead of the existing manual process. The deadline for digital filing has been set at Oct 30, 2026, in accordance with Rule 12(6) of the Civil Servants (Conduct) Rules, 2026. Under the new mechanism, officers will first have to provide their name, designation, personal active email address, mobile number and CNIC to their respective cadre administrator for creation of an account on the FBR portal. The cadre administrator will forward the officers’ details to the FBR, which will notify them about account creation through email, SMS or other prescribed means. Officers will then activate their accounts using their CNIC and a one-time password to set their own password. Once logged in, officers will find a “Declaration” option on the FBR portal dashboard. By selecting this option, they will be required to enter the requisite information through subsequent screens, with the details specified in Annex-I of the Establishment Division’s memorandum. The information submitted by officers will subsequently be subjected to risk-based verification checks by the FBR, which will communicate the results to the relevant cadre administrator. Establishment Division said selected non-sensitive sections of the declarations would be published on the FBR website for information of the general public. The declarations must be filed within the prescribed deadline, while any rectification of errors on the portal will be permissible up to Nov 30, 2026, subject to approval or authorisation of the cadre administrator concerned. Senate body orders probe into ‘overcharging’ by telco. ISLAMABAD: The Senate Standing Com­mittee on Information Technology and Tele­c­ommunication has constituted a subcommittee to investigate allegations that a leading telecom firm had charged customers Rs5.83 billion in excess of tariffs approved by the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA). The subcommittee, headed by Senator Dr Afnanullah Khan, will examine the alleged overcharging by Jazz and the regulatory action taken by the PTA in the matter. The decision was taken following a heated debate between PTA officials and representatives of the Auditor General of Pakistan (AGP). Committee Chairperson Senator Palwasha Khan intervened to pacify the situation when the PTA chairman threatened to resign if any allegation of corruption was levelled against him. Meanwhile, a Jazz spokesperson said the matter concerned two government entities and that Jazz would present its point of view if called before any relevant forum. The matter relates to the audit of the PTA for 2024. The audit objection stated that the telecom regulator had allowed a 15 per cent tariff increase for Jazz against a permissible limit of 3pc. The audit also suggested seeking the opinion of the Competition Commission of Pakistan (CCP) on the tariff policy. PTA Chairman retired Maj Gen Hafeezur Rehman questioned the proposal, saying that if tariffs were to be decided by the CCP, the PTA should not be held responsible for ensuring quality of service. “Let them take the whole responsibility,” he said. He maintained that the regulator had acted with complete transparency in allowing the 15pc tariff increase for Jazz and offered to have the matter subjected to a forensic audit. The PTA chairman categorically stated that he would resign if even one rupee of overcharging by the telecom operator was established in violation of the authority’s approved tariffs. He explained that the PTA examined mobile packages before their launch and monitored compliance with the approved tariff structure. However, audit officials had raised certain queries regarding the matter. Senator Palwasha Khan subsequently decided to constitute the subcommittee. It will examine the relevant tariff approvals, packages and billing details to determine whether customers were charged amounts beyond the rates approved by the regulator. Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

Palestine in focus. ISRAEL’S barbaric violence in Gaza, as well as rampages by extremist Jewish settlers in the West Bank, have earned the Zionist state the opprobrium of several states during the ongoing UN General Assembly. While the impassioned speeches will not be enough to stop the violence against the Palestinian people, they do indicate that even some of Israel’s allies in the West are having a difficult time justifying its monstrous behaviour. French President Emmanuel Macron said the “spectacle” in Gaza should “shame us all”. He also highlighted the grim situation in the West Bank. Similarly, Turkish President Recep Erdogan termed Gaza an “inhumane … concentration camp”. At a separate meeting on the two-state solution, Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar slammed the Israeli “machinery of occupation”. At the same event, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said “time is running out” for the two-state solution. Perhaps the outgoing UN head was being overly optimistic — Israel has done all possible to ensure a viable Palestinian state does not emerge. Not too far from these meetings the Board of Peace was also holding a session, pledging $2.45bn for Gaza’s ‘recovery’. While the promise of these funds should be welcomed, the reality in the occupied Strip tempers any hopes for Gaza’s betterment. After all, since last year’s ceasefire Israel has murdered some 1,400 people in Gaza, mostly civilians, while Tel Aviv has refused to end its occupation of the Strip, even though Hamas agreed to give up its arms. Meanwhile, illegal settlements have exploded in the West Bank, with Jewish settlers growing more vicious in their attacks by the day. Therefore, throwing money at Gaza will do little if the Palestinians remain under siege, and the theft of their land continues. If conscientious members of the international community are serious about their concern for Palestine, they must back their talk with action. Israel must be held to account for its genocidal violence in Gaza, while settlers in the West Bank should be punished for their occupation of Palestinian land, and frequent physical attacks on Arabs. All illegal settlements need to be uprooted. Sadly, while calls for a two-state solution continue, the current Israeli regime — and whatever dispensation emerges after the coming elections in the Zionist state — will remain hell-bent on preventing a sovereign Palestinian state from emerging. Meanwhile, Israel’s most powerful foreign patron — the US — seems utterly uninterested in making Tel Aviv commit itself to the peace process. PR stunts under the Board of Peace are one thing; genuine pressure on Israel to end the occupation is another. Can the Palestinian people expect relief when such powerful actors remain committed to prolonging their suffering? Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

Education for society. NOTWITHSTANDING what might be going on in other countries, Pakistan has a real problem regarding violence against women. In the past few months alone, we have seen some horrendous incidents: ‘honour’ killings, marriage-of-choice killings, rapes, domestic violence, spousal violence and killings, abduction, rape and killing of minors, and violence against employees and staff. There is no dearth of reports from national and international bodies documenting the extent and severity of these issues. A couple of points stand out in these reports. One, we do not have good data on violence against women. Incidents are underreported, and there are no national registries or data sets of any sort. Most reported data comes from newspaper reporting, police case registrations, hotline reports, and so on. Two, though many reasons — poor laws and weak implementation, few protections, pathetic institutional arrangements, low reporting and conviction rates, delays, social and societal taboos, etc — are cited in these reports, a primary one is the impact of patriarchy: the control of men over society. Patriarchy shapes not only laws, norms, and expectations in this society; it also shapes responses: what she was wearing, why she was out at that time, why she was driving, and so on. Patriarchy is hard to spot, fight, and neutralise because it is embedded in almost every norm, rule, and law. Most societies have, historically and even today, used education to address society’s main issues. What it means to be educated has varied across societies and times, and one element (other than the ability to carry out tasks) has been the larger socialisation of the individual within society and the shaping of their values and norms. I want to pose the question: should we not be shaping our education to take on the issue of patriarchy and its impacts directly? Recently, my daughter started school as a fifth-grader in a public school in London. On the very first day, after introductions and other formalities, her teacher spent a couple of hours talking about the autism spectrum and notions of inclusion, expected behaviour, and what was not expected or what would not be tolerated. This came before any conversation about the English or math curriculum. This term, the heroes the class will be introduced to include Frida Kahlo, Mahatma Gandhi, Simone Biles, and a couple of human rights defenders from across the globe. We must address the most urgent social and cultural issues of our society through education. Every day when I walk her back from school and ask her about her day, she tells me about the book they have been reading in class, the documentary they saw, the discussions they had, etc. I have to ask specifically about her math, English and history lessons. They are there, and she is learning the subjects she is supposed to, but the school and her education are much more than that. This has been true every school day. It is about what she needs as a human being and a citizen; it is about values and the kind of society that needs to be there. Specific skills are just a small part of the ‘education’ she is getting. I went to some of the best schools in Lahore in the day. But when I landed in England for undergraduate studies, one of the first things I noticed, comparing my own educational experiences with those of my undergraduate peers from England, was that almost each one of my peers had been exposed to things I had not. All of them had good exposure to and knowledge of a major European language other than English. All of them had studied music for many years in their schools, and many could play one instrument fairly well or had a good understanding of it. Many of them had had singing lessons: some were good choir singers. So, language, music and singing. Their exposure to art was also more advanced than mine. The schools I attended focused much more on doing well in academic subjects and preparing for school-leaving examinations. Though schools, especially high-fee private schools, have changed a lot, including in Pakistan over the years, even the best of them today remain narrowly focused on subject understanding and examination performance. They do not give any importance to preparing citizens and human beings. Nor is there a demand for this from parents. In fact, the trend, at least in public schools, is the opposite. With clear evidence that most children in schools are not learning enough (77 per cent are ‘learning poor’), the focus has shifted to foundational learning to ensure students grasp the basics of language and math. But the danger is that this approach narrows the scope of education even more. We focus on only essential learning objectives and try to drill them into students. We teach these and test only these. We test only these, so we teach only these. Foundational learning is the flavour right now, and it is hard even to raise concerns about what this might mean for broader educational objectives. Education has always been about creating citizens and human beings who can take us forward. We must address the most pressing social and cultural issues of our society through education. If we do not, what is the point of education, and how else can we plan for a better society? Violence against women, in all its forms, and the grip of patriarchy on our society is exactly the kind of embedded issue that cannot be tackled through law alone and has to be challenged through education and with a sense of purpose. The sheer brutality of what we keep seeing should wake us up to the urgency with which this needs to be addressed. The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums. Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

Container city. EVEN after butchering local ecologies and evicting tens of thousands from their decades-old homes, they insist on calling it Islamabad the beautiful. It really ought to be called Container City. The federal capital — and its twin city, Rawalpindi — once again resembles a loading dock for cargo ships. And as always, we are told that besieging the twin cities is in the greater national interest. The fact that official definitions of the national interest are completely unrelated to popular sentiment is not a new quandary for the powers that be. But in comparison to almost every other dispensation in Pakistan’s history, this regime is not bothered with gaining even a modicum of consent from the people, having liberally deployed the big stick in the country’s core regions to match what has always been the historical norm in the peripheries. Barely veiled threats have been issued this time too, ‘violent groups’ warned against trying to enter Islamabad. There have been a series of pre-emptive strikes against anyone and everyone that the government designates a ‘security risk’. From Imran Khan’s elderly sisters to the president of the Islamabad street vendors’ association, the regime is intent on ensuring that it alienates even those who have no link to the PTI. Whether the latter’s ‘long march’ even materialises is irrelevant, because the optics of a heavily contained population is the real story. The container city, in fact, is a microcosm of the country at large. If you have a dissenting political opinion, you can be locked up, issued a Peca notice, or maybe even disappeared. To aspire to an economic situation beyond bare survival requires one to work longer and harder for slave wages — if you are amongst those from the army of unemployed that can actually find work. The container city is a microcosm of the country at large. It should not go unnoticed that Islamabad’s police officials have asked for Rs827 million to manage the yet-to-happen protests. Meanwhile, there is no suggestion that even a pittance of that sum will be allocated to upgrade facilities and quality of services in PIMS in the wake of the horrific fire which claimed the lives of 14 newborns. There is no pretence at play here, no meaningful hegemonic strategy. The only consistent and conscious interest of the regime is in the realm of geopolitics. But unlike authoritarian rule under Ayub, Zia and Musharraf, today’s rulers cannot count on a structural windfall due to favourable geopolitical winds. Aside from acquiring geostrategic rents from anti-communist Seato and Cento pacts, the Ayub regime actually had an industrial policy, cultivating something resembling a manufacturing sector and absorbing some labouring masses displaced from the agrarian sector. The 22 families, including emergent state profiteers, may have captured the major spoils, but there was some logic to the regime’s claim that a little wealth would eventually ‘trickle down’ to the masses. Even while presiding over de-industrialisation, Zia benefited from the Gulf remittances as well as big industrial investments made under the Bhutto dispensation, not to mention windfalls from the ‘Afghan jihad’. Musharraf came to power after industrial policy was definitively declared dead, but the dictatorship nevertheless benefited from post 9/11 remittances and ‘war on terror’ dollars. The current dispensation only secures fuel to keep government running the next day by extorting the masses through a levy, while its economic imagination is limited to FDI and a developmental logic revolving around resource grabs. It has shut down border trade with Afghanistan, which is a major supply of the everyday eco­­nomy. Mean­while, members of the Pakistani bourgeoisie itself lament its comp­rador character, the CEO of the Sentinel Group recently penn­ing a telling essay on ‘Pakistan’s missing multinationals’. To be sure, the rot extends much deeper than the present regime. The so-called ‘demographic dividend’ which has been hyped up for at least 15 years is, instead, a huge pressure cooker; neither the state nor the private bourgeoisie — and for the most part this nexus operates in unison — has the capacity or interest to develop the skills of an exceedingly young population let alone guarantee it a dignified income. And where young and old working people alike demonstrate enterprise so as to make ends meet, the response of the state is to suppress, confiscate, even destroy. Look no further than the treatment of Islamabad’s katchi abadi dwellers and street vendors in recent months. Containment of the political and economic freedoms of Pakistan’s teeming masses is what the militarised state apparatus knows best. But building container cities does not make acute contradictions disappear, they only magnify them. The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad. Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

Pezeshkian says Islamabad MoU still 'fully acceptable' to Iran, ready to take it forward: PM Shehbaz. NEW YORK: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said on Thursday that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had told him the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was “fully acceptable” to Tehran even today and that they were “ready to take it forward”. The premier’s statement came after he held a “detailed” discussion with the Iranian president on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York. Earlier, a statement by the PM’s Office said that the premier stressed the importance of implementing the Islamabad MoU — a 14-point interim agreement signed between the US and Iran in June that gave a framework for ending the ongoing conflict — in the meeting. Pakistan had also signed the agreement as a mediator. The conflict, however, has since continued with sporadic strikes and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports, while Iran has maintained control over traffic through the strategic waterway. After PM Shehbaz met with Pezeshkian, he was asked by the media about the possibility of any progress on de-escalating the situation in the Middle East. The premier replied that Pakistan’s leadership united in its resolve to expedite the peace efforts under the Islamabad MoU. He also mentioned the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — two key waterways for the world’s oil fuel supply that have been affected by the conflict in the Middle East. “The current situation in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, and the provocative activities taking place there, require brotherly and friendly countries to work together to reduce tensions,” he stressed. “For this purpose, today I met the Iranian president, had a detailed meeting with him, and told him that restoring peace to the region is the need of the hour, a very important need,” he said. PM Shehbaz said Pakistan, as it had done in the past, would continue working for peace with Iran, which he described as a “brotherly” and neighbouring country. “I told him that Pakistan’s leadership, whether military or political, will, God willing, work together and continue its efforts to bring peace to the region,” he said. The premier further narrated that in his meeting with President Pezeshkian, the latter appreciated Pakistan’s efforts and reaffirmed Iran’s acceptance of the Islamabad MoU. “The Iranian president said the Islamabad MoU is still fully acceptable to us and they are ready to take it forward,” he added. The prime minister said Pakistan would continue working with friendly and brotherly countries to help reduce tensions and promote peace in the region. Earlier, the PMO statement said PM Shehbaz expressed “deep concern over the prolonged conflict and emphasised the need for restraint, de-escalation, and sustained diplomatic engagement to achieve lasting peace and stability in the region” in his meeting with Pezeshkian. “He also underscored the importance of implementing the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding and reaffirmed Pakistan’s readiness to continue playing sincere and constructive role in support of regional peace and stability,” the statement added. The two leaders discussed the evolving regional situation, with Pezeshkian appreciating Pakistan’s “principled diplomacy and concerted efforts for regional peace and security”, according to the statement. “Underlining the importance of maintaining regular consultations and close coordination to address the prevailing challenges and seize the opportunities, the two sides agreed to work for regional peace, security, and prosperity,” it said. Regarding bilateral ties, the two leaders reaffirmed the close and longstanding ties between Pakistan and Iran and underscored the need to further strengthen bilateral cooperation across all areas of mutual interest, it added. “The Iranian President also underscored the enduring strength of Pakistan-Iran relations, rooted in shared history, culture, and faith, and reaffirmed Tehran’s strong desire to further deepen multifaceted cooperation,” it said. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, and Special Assistant to the Prime Minister Tariq Fatemi were also present at the meeting, as well as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. During his interaction with the media, PM Shehbaz highlighted what he described as close cooperation between Pakistan’s political and military leadership, saying that this teamwork was contributing both to diplomatic efforts and economic stability. Asked whether he had taken the Iranian president into confidence about the Makkah Defence Alliance, the prime minister said, “Yes, this was discussed, and we did inform him.” Soon after the prime minister spoke, reporters asked Defence Minister Khawaja Asif whether Iran was on board on the Makkah accord. He said Pakistan had discussed the agreement with Iran, and that it could join the alliance in the future. The alliance’s member states, he said, were still in the process of setting up the accord’s secretariat, after which further details would be discussed. PM Shehbaz and Pezeshkian had previously held a meeting in Kyrgyzstan, on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Council of Heads of State meeting in August, during which they reaffirmed the close and longstanding ties between both countries. At the same time, PM Shehbaz had also stressed the importance of restraint and sustained diplomatic engagement to achieve lasting peace and stability in the region amid the US-Iran conflict. Thursday’s meeting with the Iranian president comes as Islamabad continues efforts to bring the United States and Iran back to the negotiating table regarding the war in the Middle East. Pezeshkian on Wednesday struck a defiant tone speaking at the UN for the first time since Washington and Israel launched an all-out war on his country, vowing Tehran would never “bend at the knee”. He made no reference to the talks to resolve the stalled war in his steely speech. However, the Iranian side earlier this week indicated its willingness to return to dialogue with the US to de-escalate tensions. The flexibility on the issue was indicated by the Iranian side in a meeting between Pezeshkian and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi during the latter’s visit to Tehran. Pakistan, meanwhile, has remained engaged in efforts to keep the diplomatic channel open. Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir has used his contacts with the US administration, while Pakistani officials have made repeated visits to Tehran. Diplomatic sources say Qatar is handling the immediate shuttle diplomacy between the US and Iran in New York, while Pakistan is working through a parallel channel with Tehran as regional efforts intensify to keep the latest diplomatic contacts from collapsing. The distinction has emerged from reporting by US and international media on the renewed US-Iran contacts around the United Nations General Assembly, with Qatar and Pakistan both involved in efforts to keep communication open between Washington and Tehran. PM Shehbaz is expected to address the UNGA on Friday.

Security forces kill several Afghan Taliban fighters in retaliatory action along Balochistan border: sources. Pakistani troops responded to an act of aggression along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border in Balochistan and killed several Afghan Taliban on Thursday, state media reported, citing sources. State-run APP reported, citing sources, that the Afghan Taliban attempted to enter the Pakistani territory in Balochistan’s Gulistan sector and carry out an act of aggression. Meanwhile, officials also reported attacks on some border posts in Pakistan. The APP report said in retaliatory action, several Afghan Taliban fighters were killed. Intermittent exchange of fire between security forces and Afghan Taliban was ongoing after midnight, according the sources cited in the report. There has been an uptick in tensions at the Pak-Afghan border lately. Pakistan conducted precision aerial and drone strikes in 10 locations across Afghanistan in retaliation for drones launched from the neighbouring country a day earlier, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said earlier in the day. The response came after eight drones, launched from Afghanistan, entered Pakistani airspace near the Torkham border and Kohat on Wednesday. Security sources said they were subsequently shot down. It was also reported that the Afghan Taliban engaged in unprovoked firing the night before near Kurram as security forces foiled an attempt by terrorists to cross into Pakistan. On Sept 21, Pakistan, in response to recent terrorist attacks in KP, conducted “calibrated” airstrikes in the border region with Afghanistan against terrorist hideouts and safe havens of terrorist organisations. A statement from the information ministry on Monday said that over 28 terrorists were eliminated in the strikes. “It is a matter of grave concern that Afghanistan continues to remain a hub of terrorism,” the ministry said at the time, specifying that the “threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan”. The airstrikes had come after a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation launched to clear the area. Ghazab lil-Haq Tarar described Pakistan’s action as part of its ongoing counter-terrorism campaign, Ghazab lil Haq. On the night of February 26, following unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban from across the border, Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab lil Haq against terrorist hideouts. Pakistan also carried out strikes in the border region with Afghanistan in late June , with the government saying they were in response to a wave of terrorist attacks, including one on a Rangers camp in Karachi . At the time, Tarar said that 25 terrorists were killed in those strikes in Paktia, Paktika and Kunar. Pakistan had carried out similar strikes on terrorist hideouts along its border with Afghanistan earlier that month, killing 26 terrorists. In July, security forces responded to unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban at border posts in Kurram, security sources had said. In the same month, the Afghan Taliban regime launched four rudimentary drones across the border into Balochistan, which were shot down by security forces. Two drones were also shot down in June in Qila Abdullah and Chagai districts. Pak-Afghan ties As clashes continue, tensions between Islamabad and Kabul have remained high. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. Earlier this week, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar addressed a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), where he called for steps towards concrete and verifiable action to prevent the use of Afghan soil for terrorism against any neighbouring country, particularly Pakistan. Dar said Pakistan was “seriously concerned” about the presence of over two dozen terrorist groups in Afghanistan that threatened regional and international peace and security. Last week, Pakistan also told the UN Security Council that it would respond to terrorist threats emanating from Afghanistan in self-defence as and when needed and in accordance with international law. Earlier this month, the Foreign Office (FO) declared that meaningful progress in relations with Kabul would depend on the Taliban taking concrete and verifiable action against Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory. It maintained that while Islamabad welcomed China’s continuing engagement, the external facilitation could not substitute for action by Kabul against terrorist infrastructure. According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from December 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group. The report also pointed to growing operational and facilitation linkages among the TTP, Al Qaeda, Islamic State-Khorasan (ISIL-K) and the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA).
