Saudi air defences intercept 6 Houthi ‘ballistic missiles’. • Rebels target Yanbu, Taif, military sites in Jazan; push to seize key Taiz-Aden supply route • Riyadh lifts warnings issued for Makkah, Jeddah, Tabuk, other regions • UN rights chief ‘appalled’ as civilian toll climbs in Yemen RIYADH: Saudi Arabia intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen’s Houthis on Thursday after issuing warnings for several regions, including the holy city of Makkah. The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government said the missiles were intercepted before reaching targets in Taif and Yanbu, a key Red Sea area important for Saudi oil exports. It was not immediately clear whether the attacks caused any damage or casualties. Saudi Civil Defence had earlier issued emergency alerts for several areas, including Makkah, Yanbu, Taif, Jeddah and Tabuk. The warnings were lifted mi­­nutes later. In recent weeks, similar ale­rts have often preceded Houthi attacks. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said in posts on X that “escalations and violations by the terrorist Houthi militia will be dealt with firmly”. The Houthis later claimed responsibility for attacks targeting Saudi military sites in Jazan province near the Yemeni border. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched a barrage involving ballistic missiles and drones aimed at what he described as operations rooms, command centers, weapons depots, missile launch sites and military camps. The latest attacks come as fighting has intensified inside Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces. At least 150 fighters from both sides were killed in the past 24 hours, according to an AFP tally based on sources from both factions. At least 98 government forces and soldiers were killed, while the Houthis said at least 52 of their fighters were killed in clashes. Many on both sides were also killed in clashes in the Kahboub Mountains and in areas between the Lahj and Taiz regions, as the Houthis seek to dominate the highlands overlooking Bab al-Mandab to protect newly seized territory. The Riyadh-backed government’s forces had earlier repelled overnight attacks by the Houthis on a key supply route to Yemen’s third biggest city Taiz from the southern port city of Aden where the internationally recognised administration is based, sources said. The Houthis have kept up pressure on government forces seeking to consolidate their power through a steep winding mountain pass. Known as Hejat al-Abd, the road is a lifeline for forces fighting on behalf of Yemen’s government, which has been hemmed in by the Houthis. The road is also critical for goods entering Taiz and its southern and western rural areas. It is the only route for residents seeking to travel abroad, with no commercial flights operating . Seizing parts of the Taiz-Aden road could allow the Houthis to tighten their grip around Taiz and deal another blow to the government. Meanwhile, the United Nations human rights chief expressed alarm Thursday over the growing civilian toll as the conflict worsens. UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said he was “appalled” by the situation, warning that civilians were suffering the consequences of the renewed fighting. “As if the people of Yemen haven’t already endured enough misery, civilians are now bearing the brunt of this latest upsurge in fighting,” Turk said, adding that “civilians must never be targeted, and their protection must be the overriding priority”. Turk’s office said at least 125 civilians had been killed or injured in Houthi attacks since the beginning of August. Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

India’s theatre command push marred by capability gaps, readiness concerns. The Modi government’s push for Integrated Theatre Commands has faced growing criticism and concerns over its implementation. The emphasis on political objectives and tight deadlines risks coming at the expense of military professionalism and could undermine the combat effectiveness of India’s armed forces across the three services. The Indian Air Force (IAF) remains the most visible victim, but critical shortages in the army and navy further expose the dangerous fragility of India’s defence posture. The Inter-Services Organisations (Command, Control and Discipline) Act, 2023, was introduced in the Lok Sabha on Mar 15, 2023, passed during the Monsoon Session and received presidential assent on Aug 15, 2023. It came into effect on May 10, 2024, while the rules were notified on May 27, 2025, granting the executive sweeping powers over joint military structures. By early 2026, Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General Anil Chauhan had submitted recommendations for three theatre commands — Northern, Western and Maritime — while a Joint Operations Centre was being prepared for operational status by the end of May under pressure to meet government deadlines before the CDS’s extended tenure ended. This politically mandated restructuring overrides professional concerns and service-specific doctrines, turning a potentially valuable reform into a high-risk gamble. The crisis within the IAF is dire. As of Apr 2026, the force operates only 29 fighter squadrons — its lowest level in decades — down from roughly 31-32 before the full retirement of the MiG-21 in September 2025 . This is well below the sanctioned strength of 42 squadrons. Each squadron fields 18-20 aircraft, giving India a total combat fleet of roughly 464-522 jets. Major platforms include 258 Russian-built Su-30MKIs, 36 French-made Rafales, more than 40 Russian MiG-29s and only 30-plus locally made Tejas Mk1 aircraft. Pakistan maintains about 25 squadrons, comprising an estimated 387-450 combat aircraft, while China deploys 66 fighter squadrons and more than 1,200 fighters. Projections suggest that the IAF could reach only 35-36 squadrons by 2035, despite orders for 141 Tejas Mk1A aircraft and procurement clearance for 114 Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft (MRFA) in February 2026. Discussions about raising the target to 54-56 squadrons highlight the scale of the gap. The strain is not limited to the air domain. The Indian Army faces persistent equipment shortfalls and manpower challenges. As of 2026, several infantry and artillery units continue to rely on outdated systems. The artillery modernisation plan remains delayed, with critical gaps in long-range precision munitions and air defence systems. Mountain warfare capabilities along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) have also been hampered by slow infrastructure development and equipment shortages, amid heightened tensions with China since the June 2020 Galwan Valley clash . The Indian Navy operates only one aircraft carrier, INS Vikramaditya, while the full operationalisation of INS Vikrant has been delayed by technical and logistical issues. Its submarine fleet has also faced significant shortfalls, with India operating only 15-16 conventional submarines, many of them ageing, against a requirement of at least 24. The number of nuclear-powered attack submarines remains limited. Destroyer and frigate numbers are insufficient for effective multi-domain operations across the vast Indian Ocean region, particularly amid China’s growing naval presence. Indigenous shipbuilding delays and budget constraints have further widened these gaps, raising questions about the Maritime Theatre Command’s preparedness even before its full implementation. The IAF has strongly resisted the permanent division of its depleted assets among the three theatre commands, warning that such fragmentation could undermine air power’s core advantage of flexibility. Similar concerns have been raised across the other two services. The army is concerned about losing operational control of assets, while the navy fears its limited blue-water capabilities could be stretched too thin. Yet pressure to proceed with the restructuring has continued despite these concerns, contributing to increased inter-service friction since the 2023 Act and the 2025 rules. Since the post of CDS was created on Jan 1, 2020, the government has outlined a series of reforms, including binding joint orders in July 2025, while planning for the restructuring was reportedly more than 90 per cent complete. However, chronic under investment, with defence spending consistently below 2.5 per cent of GDP, procurement delays and a multi-vendor fleet have continued to pose challenges for the armed forces. The gap between the reform plans and existing capabilities remains significant. With only 29 IAF squadrons, fewer than 522 combat aircraft, limited naval platforms and delays in army modernisation, questions remain over the pace at which India can strengthen its overall military capabilities. The accelerated 2026 restructuring could have long-term strategic implications. Without corrective measures, including substantially increased defence spending, addressing critical shortages across the services, avoiding the forced division of assets and building greater professional consensus, the Integrated Theatre Commands could face significant operational and strategic challenges.

Delegate walkout, protests greet Netanyahu as he addresses UN General Assembly. NEW YORK: Dozens of delegates walked out of the UN General Assembly hall on Thursday as hundreds of protesters gathered outside the building while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended Tel Aviv’s actions amid growing international isolation, with elections looming that could threaten his political future. The walkout undersco­red the competing pressu­res facing Netanyahu, who is battling mounting criticism abroad over the Gaza conflict while campaigning for re-election at home ahead of an October 27 vote. On Thursday, Netanyahu delivered a combative address inside the General Assembly, where dozens of delegations walked out as he began speaking. The departing diplomats left large sections of the hall empty, creating a striking contrast with Netanyahu’s attempt to use the podium to present Israel’s case before the international community. Netanyahu responded by accusing his critics of hypocrisy and calling them “moral cowards.” He rejected allegations that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, saying Israel had prevented rather than committed genocide. He defended the country’s military actions in Gaza and elsewhere in the region. Delegates walk out of the General Assembly hall as Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrives to address the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, US, September 24. — Reuters He also devoted a significant part of his speech to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, calling him “the antisemitic mayor of New York” and accusing him of spreading what Netanyahu described as lies about Israel. Mamdani, who had declined to join the street protests, responded after the speech. “Prime Minister Netanyahu used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitise his genocide of Palestinians,” Mamdani said. “No lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity.” Mamdani previously said New York City lacked the authority to enforce the ICC warrant against Netanyahu, arguing that the appropriate authorities should carry it out. On Wednesday night, the mayor had hosted Palestinian families from Gaza at Gracie Mansion and planted an olive tree with them, saying: “May peace be our future.” The two scenes — protesters confronting his government’s policies on the streets and diplomats leaving the hall during his address — turned Netanyahu’s brief visit to New York into a day of parallel confrontation. Netanyahu’s stay had already been sharply shortened amid security concerns and expectations of protests. He arrived on Thursday morning, addressed the General Assembly and was scheduled to return to Israel the same evening rather than remain in New York overnight. Outside the UN, Jewish and Muslim activists, Palestinian supporters, human-rights campaigners, progressive Jewish groups, politicians, artists and musicians took part in separate demonstrations across Manhattan. Their messages varied, but opposition to Netanyahu’s government and Israel’s conduct of the Gaza war brought many of them into the streets at the same time. Demonstrators protest after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the United Nations 81st General Assembly in New York City, U.S., September 24. — Reuters The protests also offered a visible glimpse of a generational shift in American attitudes toward Israel and Netanyahu. While support for Israel remains stronger among older Americans, younger Americans have become substantially more critical of the Israeli government. A Pew Research Centre survey conducted in May found that only 18 per cent of Americans aged 18 to 29 had a favourable view of the Israeli government, compared with 47pc among those aged 65 and older. Among the youngest Americans, 58pc expressed a favourable view of Palestinians, compared with 47pc among those 65 and older. That generational divide was visible on the streets of New York, where many of the demonstrators were young people, including students, activists, artists and younger politicians. The largest direct action outside the UN was organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, whose New York chapter brought hundreds of protesters to First Avenue and 39th Street. Demonstrators wearing matching white T-shirts sat in the roadway, chanting against Netanyahu and calling for an end to US support for Israel. For a while, protesters stood and sat in the street, linking arms and blocking traffic as police moved in to clear the roadway. The chants continued as officers began making arrests. At least 30 people, including actors and politicians, were arrested in the initial action. Police later said more than 100 protesters had been taken into custody. Among those detained were actors Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder, congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and City Council member Chi Ossé. Musicians Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus and actor Elliott Page were also among the prominent figures taking part in the protests. Chelsea Manning, who joined the protest, said people outside government institutions needed ways to reject policies they regarded as imperialism, ethnic cleansing and genocide. “We can’t be in there. This is the closest that we can get,” she said. Manijeh Moradian, a university professor of Iranian and Jewish heritage who participated in the demonstration, said protesters had a responsibility to speak out against what was happening in Gaza with US support. Jewish groups divided The demonstrations also highlighted divisions within New York’s Jewish community. Progressive Jewish organisations, including New York Jewish Agenda, T’ruah, J Street, New Jewish Narrative, New Israel Fund and Partners for Progressive Israel, held a separate protest at Dag Hammarskjöld Plaza near the UN. “We are gathered here as American Jews, Israelis, New Yorkers, to say: You are not welcome here,” said Margo Hughes-Robinson, executive director of New York Jewish Agenda. T’ruah, a rabbinic human-rights organisation, called for a ceasefire and accountability for alleged war crimes. The organisers described their rally as an alternative for Jewish New Yorkers who opposed Netanyahu’s policies while retaining concern for Israel and Jewish security. They were confronted by pro-Netanyahu counter-protesters who blew whistles, used megaphones, chanted “Bibi”, and sang Israel’s national anthem. On the other side, the ultra-Orthodox anti-Zionist group Neturei Karta also demonstrated, arguing that opposition to Israel could not automatically be equated with antisemitism. Elsewhere, Jewish and Muslim demonstrators marched together towards the UN, while Palestinian activists and other organisations joined the broader mobilisation against Netanyahu. A city divided over Israel and Gaza As police loaded detained protesters onto buses outside the UN, Netanyahu was speaking inside a building protected by heavy security. Outside, demonstrators sought to challenge the Israeli prime minister’s account of the Gaza war; inside, diplomats expressed their opposition by leaving the chamber. The contrast was difficult to miss. For several hours on Thursday, New York’s streets and the UN General Assembly hall became parallel stages for the same international argument — one expressed through demonstrations and arrests outside, the other through a diplomatic boycott inside. And beneath both scenes was a changing American debate over Israel.

Dar, Saudi and Turkish counterparts review progress on institutionalising tripartite defence pact. Its inaugural meeting was held on Aug 31, where officials from all member states met in Istanbul to establish the institutional structure of the alliance, and Pakistan was picked to head its secretariat in Riyadh. It added that the three sides reviewed progress on the establishment of the general secretariat, committees, and working groups, as well as “preparations for the commencement of their activities”. The three also exchanged views on the prevailing situation in the region and underscored the “importance of upholding the principles of international law, good neighbourliness, mutual respect for state sovereignty, non-interference in internal affairs, and ensuring the security and freedom of maritime navigation”. The three sides reiterated their determination to work towards peace and stability in the region and push for peaceful solutions to existing crises, the Saudi Foreign Ministry said. A day earlier, Saudi Arabia intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen’s Houthis after issuing warnings for several regions, including the holy city of Makkah. 'Nobody is working on the actual solution, which is the mindset change': India rape cases turn focus back onto women's safety. A string of rape cases in India has reignited debate over women’s safety and raised questions about why sweeping legal reforms and tougher punishments have failed to curb sexual violence. Hundreds of students marched through the streets of New Delhi on Wednesday, shouting slogans and holding placards demanding stronger safety measures following the latest high-profile case. In that incident on Monday, three men posing as police officers allegedly gang-raped a 17-year-old girl in a public park in the heart of the capital city, according to authorities. The case evokes the 2012 gang rape and murder of a 23-year-old physical therapy student on a bus, which triggered nationwide protests and led to more robust laws against sexual violence. But campaigners say those changes, which included a broadening of the definition of sexual offences and the introduction of stronger punishments for rape, have proven inadequate. “Nobody is working on the actual solution, which is the mindset change,” women’s rights activist Yogita Bhayana told AFP . “The mentality (is still) that it is a woman’s fault to be out of home late, or men policing women if they are seen with another man,” she said. “It is outrageous that society still thinks this way.” India recorded an average of 80 rape cases per day in 2024, according to the latest available official data. That compares with around 68 per day in 2012, the last year before the stronger laws came in. Activists say the true number of sexual assaults is likely far higher because many victims never file a report, often fearing stigma in a deeply patriarchal society. Lack of enforcement The alleged assault on Monday followed the rape and murder of a 16-year-old girl whose body was found by police in a decomposed state, and the alleged rape of a 17-year-old girl by a bus driver and a conductor who offered her a lift during heavy rain. Both cases occurred in recent weeks in Delhi — often called India’s “rape capital” — but other regions are not immune, with a video that surfaced this month showing a teenage girl being sexually assaulted in the eastern state of Bihar. Each case has brought arrests, political condemnation and a public outcry. After the watershed 2012 case — the woman is known nationally as “Nirbhaya” or “Fearless”, as Indian law does not allow the press to publish a rape victim’s name — the government expanded the criminal definitions of penetration and consent. Gang rape became punishable by at least 20 years in prison, and the death sentence was introduced for repeat rape offenders. Lawyers and activists say the challenge lies in enforcement. Overstretched police forces and courts lack the means to investigate cases thoroughly enough, hindering the reforms’ impacts, criminal lawyer Shilpi Jain, who has represented survivors of sexual violence, told AFP . “The problem is not in the law but with the people who are implementing it,” she said. “Overworked judges. Overworked cops. One police station handles 200,000 to 300,000 people. How will it work? This is a vicious cycle.” India’s conviction rate for rape has remained largely stable since 2012, hovering at around a quarter of all cases that make it to trial. But the criminal justice system struggles with a vast case backlog. Less than 10 per cent of the more than 200,000 rape cases before the courts in 2024 were actually completed, according to official data. “An average rape case takes seven to eight years. If the case goes to the Supreme Court, then 20 years, so criminals lose fear of law and victims lose hope,” Jain said. For gender rights activist Poonam Muttreja, legal reforms alone cannot solve a problem rooted in social attitudes and inequality. Deep-seated cultural taboos and political resistance have hampered the effectiveness of government programmes to raise awareness of sexual violence, experts say. “Prevention must begin much before a crime is committed: in homes, schools, communities, digital spaces and police systems,” Muttreja said.

Ten Challenges for the UN in 2026-2027 eschelhaas Mon, 09/14/2026 - 10:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Candidates for United Nations Secretary-General position participate in a debate at the UN General Assembly Hall in New York, on July 23, 2026. Leonardo MUNOZ / AFP Special Briefing 15 / Multilateral Diplomacy 14 September 2026 20+ minutes Ten Challenges for the UN in 2026-2027 As the 2026 General Assembly begins, the UN remains hobbled by cost cutting and big-power wrangling. The new Secretary-General to be chosen soon cannot cure all that ails the organisation, but much can be done to put its still considerable capacity to work. Leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly will find an organisation in need of revival. UN diplomacy aimed at halting wars and easing civilian suffering remains paralysed, while funding cuts have weakened UN capacity. States have one eye to the future as they prepare to appoint a new Secretary-General. Why does it matter? The UN remains the only universal forum for global cooperation on war and peace, even as the international order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope the next Secretary-General can help the organisation dispel its malaise and forge a new direction. What should be done? A new Secretary-General cannot resolve the world’s crises overnight, but this person should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capabilities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. I. Overview When world leaders last met at the UN General Assembly in September 2025, the organisation was in disarray, reeling from U.S. aid freezes and major-power disputes. A year on, the organisation remains trapped in an open-ended crisis, even after an additional round of cost cutting and other reforms. Under the Trump administration, the U.S. has morphed from a flawed champion of the international legal order into an overt scofflaw. While the U.S. has not repudiated the multilateral system anchored by the UN, it has done great damage to the organisation, insisting on shrinking multilateral peace operations, slow-rolling funding and tried to impose its ideological agenda. The Security Council continues to be a forum for hashing out big-power differences – with the U.S., Russia and China coming to agreement on second-tier files. But as regards the most salient peace and security challenges today – the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, as well as Ukraine and Sudan – the UN is notable mainly for being stuck. The next Secretary-General cannot cure all that ails the UN, but creative diplomacy could be useful in putting its still considerable capacity to work. If the overall mood at the UN is one of drifting toward perdition, it is partly because everyone is waiting for change at the top of the system. Secretary-General António Guterres will complete his term at the end of December. A small batch of candidates – eight, at the time of writing – have been publicly and privately lobbying throughout the year to replace him. Most have been cautious in their campaigning, to avoid offending the major powers that dominate the selection process. UN insiders are watching with mixed feelings. Some hope that the next Secretary-General can bring new energy to the organisation and, assuming Washington is amenable, restore a measure of political relevance and financial stability. Others worry that the U.S., China and Russia will connive to choose a weak candidate firmly under their control and that the Trump administration will force the next UN chief to make even more radical cuts throughout the institution. The selection process has at least focused minds on what the UN, multilateral cooperation and international law exist to achieve. Many member states have emphasised that they would like to see the incoming Secretary-General do more to promote conflict prevention and resolution, which Guterres has sometimes given short shrift while pursuing other goals, such as international cooperation on artificial intelligence. Guterres no doubt felt that he had little to gain by focusing on geopolitical crises given the lack of consensus among the big powers. But there is now a widespread sense that the UN cannot pretend to be a useful platform for discussions of far-reaching issues like AI if governments do not believe that it can deliver on its core, UN Charter-defined purpose of maintaining peace and security. The crises of the last twelve months have also offered reminders of the extent to which the UN still offers a necessary if imperfect scaffolding for international cooperation. The Trump administration has grudgingly turned to the Security Council to endorse its conflict management efforts in Haiti and Gaza. Faced with the fallout of the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, such as closure of the Strait of Hormuz, governments around the world have stressed the importance of international legal principles including the prohibition of aggressive war, rules protecting civilians and civilian objects in conflict, and freedom of navigation. Though the UN has had a vanishingly small voice in diplomacy aimed at ending the Middle East war, both U.S. and Iranian officials have acknowledged that the Security Council should play some role – if only a ministerial one – in any peace deal. The UN ... remains best positioned to deliver humanitarian aid, mount peace operations and manage protracted crises that few other actors ... can handle. These are small consolations, but at a moment in which the U.S. and Russia are learning the limits of hard power in the Middle East and Ukraine, there is still space to reiterate the case for diplomacy, cooperation and respect for law. The next UN Secretary-General can make it. While it is foolish to expect a single administrator, however senior, to save the world, many small and midsize UN member states, as well as many major-power officials, are ready to heed a call to reinforce the lapsing international legal order. The UN also remains best positioned to deliver humanitarian aid, mount peace operations and manage protracted crises that few other actors – including the flailing U.S.-backed Board of Peace – can handle. It is possible that new leadership at the UN can give the organisation as a whole, and its peace and security pillar in particular, a new strategic direction. But amid deadly violence, regional rifts and institutional headaches, it is a near certainty that UN crisis management will continue to involve a great deal of firefighting and muddling through. This briefing, based on Crisis Group’s research at the UN and in the countries concerned, offers a guide to some of the most urgent issues. II. The Year in Review: Trends in UN Diplomacy The UN spent much of the past year adapting to a more assertive and transactional U.S. administration. Alongside long-running crises in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, the latest U.S.-Israeli war with Iran placed additional strain on Council diplomacy and the UN-backed international order. 1 Crisis Group Special Briefing N°14, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Power , 8 July 2026. Meanwhile, the UN’s multi-year liquidity crisis worsened, compounded by the U.S. aid cuts, disrupting operations at headquarters in New York and in the field. Steep reductions in voluntary contributions to UN humanitarian agencies forced the organisation to make difficult choices with its assistance, leaving many civilians affected by armed conflict with little support. Debates over the UN’s future simmered as member states began their search for the next Secretary-General. A year after Donald Trump’s return to the White House, the organisation was no longer in shock but adjusting to a new normal. A. Crisis Management and UN Diplomacy 1. The Security Council A year ago, Crisis Group observed that U.S. diplomacy at the Security Council under the newly installed Trump administration had lacked a clear direction. 2 Crisis Group Special Briefing N°13, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2025-2026 , 9 September 2025. The arrival of U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz in New York on the eve of the 2025 UN General Assembly marked the beginning of a more purposeful, and often determined, U.S. approach in the Council. Together with Panama, the U.S. secured Council authorisation for a new Gang Suppression Force for Haiti shortly after Waltz’s arrival, along with a UN logistics office to defray some of the Force’s costs (see Section III.4). 3 “ Haiti: Vote on a Draft Resolution Authorizing a ‘Gang Suppression Force’ and a UN Support Office* ”, Security Council Report, 30 September 2025; Daniel Forti, “ New Force to Battle Haiti’s Gangs Gets Security Council Blessing ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 1 October 2025; Crisis Group Latin America & Caribbean Report N°110, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , 15 December 2025. Less than two months later, the Trump administration – backed by its regional partners and Palestine – persuaded the Council to endorse its ceasefire plan for Gaza and establish the vaguely defined Board of Peace. 4 “Resolution 2803”, UNSC S/RES/2803, 17 November 2025; Daniel Forti, Richard Gowan and Max Rodenbeck, “ What to Look for as the Gaza Peace Plan Comes to the UN Security Council ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 November 2025. In both cases, the Council agreed to arrangements that concentrated decision-making authority in Washington and minimised the UN’s political and operational roles. With UN diplomacy on the war in Gaza lowered to a simmer (see Section III.3), the U.S.-Iran conflict became the Council’s defining crisis of the past year. Major-power tensions over Iran were already high at the UN prior to the outbreak of hostilities at the end of February. After the breakdown of nuclear diplomacy between the U.S. and Iran in 2025 and the twelve-day campaign launched by Israel (and joined by the U.S.) against Iran in June, France, Germany and the UK – three of the participants in the 2015 nuclear deal, or Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action – decided to reimpose “snapback” sanctions on Tehran that were otherwise set to expire that October. 5 Naysan Rafati and Daniel Forti, “ Iran Sanctions Snapback at the UN ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 25 August 2026. Beijing and Moscow rejected the legality of the reimposed UN sanctions, and in protest, they have obstructed business in all of the Council’s sanctions committees and thematic working groups since 2026 began. 6 China and Russia have blocked the appointment of the chairs and vice chairs of all subsidiary bodies, which require Council unanimity according to the body’s informal working methods. The chairs and vice chairs are responsible for leading each body’s meetings, briefing the Council on behalf of each body and managing its workflow. For more, see “ In Hindsight: A Second Year of Delays in the Allocation of Subsidiary Body Chairs ”, Security Council Report, 1 July 2026; Letter from the Security Council’s ten elected members , UNSC S/2026/636, 30 July 2026. Tensions in the Council gradually escalated after the U.S. and Israel once again attacked Iran on 28 February. Tensions in the Council gradually escalated after the U.S. and Israel once again attacked Iran on 28 February. China and Russia sharply criticised the two states during the Council’s first emergency meeting on the war. But even so they allowed passage of a Bahrain-led resolution condemning Iran’s retaliatory fire at its Gulf Arab neighbours days later, abstaining instead of vetoing it. Their posture suggested that preserving relations with the Gulf states was a higher priority than blocking a one-sided resolution that had no teeth. 7 Beijing and Moscow abstained from the vote. Russia also submitted a separate counter-resolution discussing the war’s root causes that got too few votes to be adopted. See “ Resolution 2817 ”, UNSC S/RES/2817, 11 March 2026. Their stances gradually hardened, however, as Washington pressed the Security Council to consider more coercive measures against Tehran. In early April, the Gulf states and the U.S. tabled a resolution for the Council to endorse a vaguely defined multinational naval coalition that would be tasked with reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Moscow and Beijing vetoed the text despite intense lobbying by Gulf capitals, arguing that the resolution would have given the U.S. open-ended authorisation to escalate its campaign. 8 The vote took place hours after U.S. President Donald Trump shared a social media message threatening to annihilate Iran. During its explanation of vote, Russia invoked the Security Council’s 2011 open-ended authorisation of NATO-led military action in Libya as a comparison to the proposed Gulf-U.S. initiative. Crisis Group interviews, UN diplomats, April-May 2026. See also remarks by the Russian Federation, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10130th meeting of the United Nations Security Council”, UNSC S/PV.10130, 7 April 2026. Weeks later, the U.S. and Gulf states drafted another resolution to demand that Iran open and demine the strait, while threatening sanctions for non-compliance. Despite finding over 138 co-sponsors, the U.S. and Bahrain did not submit the text for a vote, as they could not secure the support of Russia and China. Council diplomacy on the file has since stalled. Complex and sometimes volatile relations among the U.S., China, and Russia continue to shape the boundaries of Council diplomacy beyond the Gulf. After the reversal of U.S. Ukraine policy in early 2025, when the Trump administration stopped sending arms to Kyiv to resist Russia’s all-out invasion, Moscow may have expected Washington to press the Ukrainian government to make concessions in negotiations to end the fighting. Instead, U.S. statements in the Security Council have criticised Russia’s full-scale invasion and called on the Kremlin to agree to an immediate ceasefire. 9 Remarks by the United States, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10166th Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10166, 8 June 2026. More often than not, U.S. and Russian diplomats have sparred over UN responses to crises in the Middle East and Africa. By contrast, Washington and Beijing have shown willingness to strike occasional deals in the Security Council. Though they frequently clash, recent Council action has depended on a degree of cooperation between these geopolitical rivals. In September 2025, the U.S. agreed to pay nearly $680 million to the UN peacekeeping budget and drop its objections to China becoming penholder on the Council’s Afghanistan file in exchange for Beijing’s support for the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti. 10 Daniel Forti and Richard Gowan, “ Reading the Signals of China’s U.N. Security Council Role in the Afghanistan Mission Renewal ”, Just Security , 31 July 2026. U.S. diplomats also convinced their Chinese counterparts to support the delisting of Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa and Interior Minister Anas Khattab from the UN counter-terrorism sanctions list despite Beijing’s reservations. 11 Maya Ungar, “ UN Lifts Sanctions on Syria’s President as White House Visit Beckons ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 7 November 2025. More recently, China and the U.S. collaborated to streamline the mandate of the UN political office in Afghanistan and approved each other’s candidates for leadership posts in UN missions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and South Sudan. Other Council members have found it harder to haggle with – much less criticise – the Trump administration’s adventurism. For the UK, France and many of the Council’s ten elected members, the importance of preserving bilateral relations with Washington has often quashed the temptation to toss rhetorical barbs at their U.S. counterparts. The repressed anger was most evident during the Council’s first meeting in January, an emergency session called shortly after the U.S. abducted former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, when many diplomats stopped short of censuring the Trump administration by name or condemning its action, though many took the view that the raid contravened international law. 12 “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10085th Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10084, 5 January 2026; Richard Gowan, “ Trump May Not Need a ‘Board of Peace.’ He Has the U.N. Under His Thumb ”, World Politics Review , 17 March 2026. Less than two months later, a majority of Council members only obliquely chastised the U.S. and Israel for their strikes on Iran, though many again saw the bombing as contravening the international legal order. 13 In addition to China and Russia, elected members Colombia and Pakistan also expressed strong reservations about the war. Richard Gowan, “ UN Security Council Members Limit Criticism of U.S. over Iran ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 2 March 2026. U.S. and French diplomats had a public spat at the end of July following the General Assembly’s re-election of Volker Türk as UN human rights commissioner, but the animosity has not lingered. 14 The U.S. was one of ten states to oppose Türk’s re-election in the 24 July UN General Assembly vote. In response, the Permanent Mission of France to the UN in Geneva criticised the Trump administration in a social media post by saying, “The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore”. Tweet by the French Permanent Mission to the UN in Geneva, @FranceONUGeneve, 1:12pm, 25 July 2026. In response, U.S. diplomats accused France of “disingenuous grandstanding” and walked out of the Security Council’s 27 July meeting on Ukraine as the French Permanent Representative to the UN delivered the country’s statement. See remarks by U.S. alternate representative to the UN, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10202nd Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10202, 27 July 2026. London and Paris have tended to lobby Washington behind the scenes when they disagreed with the U.S. in Council debates. They avoided a showdown in the Council on the fourth anniversary of Russia’s all-out aggression against Ukraine in February, in contrast to a major row over a U.S. resolution calling for a rapid peace deal the year before, though U.S. and European diplomats still wrangled briefly over a General Assembly resolution in support of Ukraine. 15 Richard Gowan, “ UN Vote Shows Enduring but Uneven International Support for Ukraine ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 25 February 2026. The elected members’ divergent interests have also played a prominent role in shaping Council dynamics. The elected members’ divergent interests have also played a prominent role in shaping Council dynamics. Unusually, several elected members have found themselves directly implicated in issues before the Council in 2026 to date. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Somalia sought to preserve ties with the U.S. while influencing Council discussions on conflicts in their own countries. 16 Kinshasa has used its elected term on the Security Council to raise the profile of the conflict in the eastern DRC, while Mogadishu has sought to end the Council’s engagement with the war in Somalia. Denmark and Panama, meanwhile, have had to contend with Trump’s threats to annex Greenland and seize the Panama Canal, even as they maintained working relations with U.S. diplomats in New York. Bahrain assumed a more prominent role following Iran’s attacks on Gulf states, in close coordination with Washington. Colombia (under President Gustavo Petro, now out of office) and Pakistan, by contrast, have taken more critical positions on U.S. military actions. Whereas previous cohorts of elected members had found common ground in pressing Washington for a ceasefire in Gaza, the present elected ten are less unified in how to conduct diplomacy with Washington. As for UN peace operations, where Washington sees clear strategic interests at stake, such as in the DRC and South Sudan, it has been willing to preserve UN missions and, at times, moderate its normally reflexive opposition to human rights, gender and climate-related activities – including where it has been stubborn in other mandate negotiations in the Security Council and General Assembly. More often, the U.S. has sought to scale back UN operations, claiming concerns about their effectiveness and costs. Over the past year, it has pressed the Council to narrow the mandates of UN missions in Abyei (a disputed territory on the border between Sudan and South Sudan), the Central African Republic (see Section III.5), Colombia, Kosovo and Western Sahara, while supporting the closure of the UN mission in Yemen’s port city of Hodeida. 17 “ Yemen: Vote on Final Mandate Renewal of UNMHA ”, Security Council Report, 25 January 2026. It has also signalled its intention to terminate the mandate of the UN Support Office in Somalia, which provides logistical support to the African Union troops fighting Al-Shabaab, at the end of 2026. 18 Faisal Ali, David Lewis and Giulia Paravinci, “ Somalia peacekeeping mission at risk as US blocks UN support, sources say ”, Reuters, 2 July 2026. Despite U.S. scepticism, several Council members have mounted spirited defences of UN operations. During discussions to renew the mandate of the UN mission in South Sudan, European and African Council members succeeded in stopping the U.S. from deleting swathes of the UN peacekeeping operation’s mandate language on the political process and reducing the mission’s troop ceiling by several thousands. In late 2025, the Council’s three African members and Guyana (known as the A3 Plus coalition), together with China, Russia and Pakistan, were able to nix Washington’s proposal to predicate the renewal of the mandate for the UN peacekeeping force in Abyei on a series of harsh benchmarks. 19 “ UN Interim Security Force for Abyei: Vote on Mandate Renewal Resolution* ”, Security Council Report, 13 November 2025. Denmark and Pakistan (which work together in 2026 as an informal “peacekeeping duo”) negotiated intensely with U.S. counterparts to secure support for a thematic resolution to improve the UN’s accountability measures when its peacekeepers are harmed while serving in missions. 20 “ Resolution 2823 ”, UNSC S/RES/2823, 23 June 2026. South Korea, an elected member on the Council in 2024-2025, was the third member of this grouping, which previously was known as the “peacekeeping trio”. Crisis Group interviews, UN diplomats, May-June 2026. These examples suggest that when members show unity and coordination – and when they are not confronting what Washington sees as its core interests – they can sometimes engage in effective diplomacy with the U.S. 2. The Secretary-General Secretary-General Guterres has spent much of his final year in office trying to forestall the UN’s urgent financial crisis (discussed below), complete reforms under the UN80 initiative that he launched in 2025 and defend the UN Charter in response to violations by two permanent members, Russia and the U.S. 21 The UN80 initiative, launched by Guterres in March 2025, is premised on three separate reform processes. The first is premised on budget cuts and cost savings at the UN Secretariat; the second features a review of all inter-governmental mandates; and the third is anchored in proposals for larger institutional reforms (including proposals to merge different UN agencies and offices). “ UN80 Initiative ”, UN, August 2026. Neither Moscow nor Washington is eager to engage with him personally, curtailing his opportunities to pursue new diplomatic efforts. But the Secretary-General’s cautious outlook toward UN-led conflict management has left many diplomats and officials searching for a successor who will put the organisation’s work on peace and security front and centre. The Secretary-General’s limited influence over the past year has not always been due to a lack of initiative. Shortly after the resumption of hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, Guterres appealed for creating a humanitarian corridor to permit the passage of fuel and fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz, established a UN mechanism modelled on the Black Sea Grain Initiative to facilitate these efforts and appointed a personal envoy to boost the UN’s diplomatic response. 22 “ Note to Correspondents: on the Strait of Hormuz ”, UN, 27 March 2026. His focus on the war’s global consequences won plaudits but failed to have meaningful impact, as neither the Gulf states nor the U.S. showed serious interest in reopening the strait, except in full and without condition. The initiative has faded from memory even as the war has reignited and traffic through the waterway remains constrained. 23 Guterres shared a brief update about the UN mechanism at a 24 August press conference. See “ Secretary-General’s Press Encounter – On the United Nations’ Efforts to Uphold Navigational Rights and Freedoms ”, Office of the UN Secretary-General, 24 August 2026. Elsewhere, Guterres has deployed his dwindling political capital selectively. At the end of July, he travelled to Cyprus to revive his long-running mediation between Greek and Turkish Cypriots. He also made personal appeals to Sudan’s belligerents in support of a proposed humanitarian ceasefire in Darfur. The Secretary-General continued to press for Security Council reform, including at a high-level summit convened by France and Kenya in May, and in August he released a long-awaited review of UN peace operations mandated by the 2024 Pact for the Future (see Section III.9). 24 “ Review on the future of all forms of United Nations Peace Operations ”, UNGA A/80/798 – UNSC S/2026/600, 22 July 2026. Yet meaningful progress on these and other such priorities has eluded him. B. UN Reform The UN’s financial outlook has deteriorated sharply over the past year, largely due to Washington’s failure to pay its fair share. Since President Trump returned to office, the U.S. has ponied up only a portion of the nearly $4 billion in dues it owes the organisation. 25 In late August, the U.S. agreed to make a payment of $725 million to the UN regular budget, an amount reportedly calculated by Washington to avoid losing its vote in the General Assembly under Article 19 of the UN Charter. The U.S. is not the only member state withholding its obligatory dues, even if it is the largest and has accumulated the most arrears. China has regularly delayed its annual payments to the UN regular budget – in 2026 paying only at the beginning of September – though it traditionally does not accumulate arrears. See Catherine Pollard, “ Financial situation of the United Nations ”, statement to the Fifth Committee of the General Assembly at its 80th Session, 7 May 2026; “ Chandramouli Ramanathan (UN Controller) & others on the UN Budget ”, Office of the UN Spokesperson, 1 July 2026; Humeyra Pamuk and Emma Farge, “ US plans $725 million payment towards its large UN debt ”, Reuters, 21 August 2026. U.S. officials have openly stated their intention to place the UN on a starvation diet and withdrawn from several UN bodies. 26 “ Withdrawing the United States from International Organizations, Conventions and Treaties that Are Contrary to the Interests of the United States ”, White House, 7 January 2026; Emma Farge, Olivia Le Poidevin, Simon Lewis and David Brunnstrom, “ Diplomatic efforts seek to avert Trump split with UN refugee agency, sources say ”, Reuters, 21 July 2026. Yet, to the relief of many diplomats and UN officials, Washington no longer appears intent on a wholesale retreat from the organisation. Since the end of 2025, it has provided nearly $5 billion in voluntary funding to Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), UNICEF and the World Food Programme, agencies that have embraced the administration’s reform agenda and retained bipartisan support in Congress. While these contributions have been critical in sustaining key UN operations, they remain well below Washington’s historical level of support and are heavily earmarked to align with U.S. priorities. 27 “ OCHA-Managed Humanitarian Funds Receive Landmark US$2 Billion Contribution from United States ”, UN OCHA, 29 December 2025; “ United States Pledges Additional $1.8 Billion in Life-Saving Humanitarian Funding to OCHA’s Humanitarian Reset & Shares Powerful Results from the Trump Administration’s UN Humanitarian Reform Agreement ”, U.S. Department of State, 14 May 2026; “ United States Announces More Than $1 Billion in Assistance to UNICEF and World Food Program to Address Global Humanitarian Needs ”, U.S. Department of State, 16 June 2026. Diplomats have also welcomed the Secretary-General’s willingness to propose structural reforms to the UN system but have baulked at specific proposals to merge various UN agencies (see Section III.8), often due to a mix of national interests (which could involve political or financial ties to a specific office) and principled concerns that the changes could weaken the UN’s work in these areas. 33 Smaller organisational changes have already taken place, including the creation of the UN’s Peacebuilding and Peace Support Operations Office, merging units within the UN’s Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and the Department of Peace Operations. C. The Search for a New Secretary-General The process of choosing Guterres’ successor, which began in November 2025, is approaching a crescendo. Members of the Security Council held their first straw poll at the end of July, and they will continue to take these informal soundings until one candidate receives at least nine votes from the fifteen-member body with no objection from any of the five permanent members. Ten Challenges for the UN Even as the UN is mired in interlocking difficulties, the organisation can still contribute to conflict resolution and crisis management in many domains. The following list features countries and issue areas where the UN confronts either major challenges or opportunities in the year ahead. It is intended to demonstrate the myriad factors affecting how the UN and its member states respond to conflicts and emergencies around the world. The list is not exhaustive, however, and it excludes cases that Crisis Group has highlighted elsewhere or in years past, such as Afghanistan, the DRC, South Sudan, Ukraine and others. 1. Continuing UN engagement in southern Lebanon In August 2025, the U.S. and Israel strong-armed the Security Council into shutting down the UN peacekeeping mission in southern Lebanon (UNIFIL) – first established in 1978 and significantly upgraded by Resolution 1701 twenty years ago – by the end of 2026 (though the phased withdrawal of troops will extend considerably past 31 December). 50 “ Resolution 2790 ”, UNSC S/RES/2790, 28 August 2025. While questions about southern Lebanon have long vexed the Council, the latest conflagration between Israel and Hizbollah raises the stakes even higher. 51 Heiko Wimmen and David Wood, “ Entrenching a Meaningful Israel-Lebanon Ceasefire ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 19 June 2026. The danger is now that the UN will terminate its 48-year blue helmet operation without clarity on what kind of international presence, if any, might follow. Much will now depend on the trajectory of U.S.-backed negotiations between Israel and Lebanon, which to date have failed to produce a viable security arrangement. The two states signed a “framework agreement” on 26 June, under which the Lebanese army is to assert control of “pilot zones” in southern Lebanon, ensuring that Hizbollah no longer has a military footprint in these areas. 52 “ Trilateral Framework Between the United States of America, the State of Israel and the Republic of Lebanon ”, U.S. Department of State, 26 June 2026. Yet the scheme, which is meant to “serve as the mechanism for phased and verified (Israeli) redeployments”, has already run into trouble. 53 Ibid. Lebanon complains that Israel has kept attacking Lebanese territory, including with lethal airstrikes and the systematic destruction of villages, and authorised “pilot zones” only in areas that it never occupied. Israeli officials, for their part, make Hizbollah’s full disarmament a condition for the Israeli army’s withdrawal. 54 Maayan Lubell and Maya Gebeily, “ After US criticism, Israel ties Lebanon withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament ”, Reuters, 13 August 2026. Beirut officially outlawed Hizbollah’s military activities in March, but, in practice, it cannot risk trying to compel the group to disarm. 55 Lebanese political and military leaders have resisted calls to deploy the Lebanese army to confront Hizbollah by force. They fear that such a move could trigger disastrous domestic consequences, such as the military fracturing along sectarian lines. Crisis Group Middle East Briefing N°94, Containing Domestic Tensions in War-hit Lebanon , 27 February 2025. See also Michael Young, “ Pushing Beirut into an armed conflict with Hezbollah is insane ”, Diwan (blog), Carnegie Middle East Center, 14 May 2026. Even if the terms of the deal were to be spelled out more precisely, the belligerents would almost certainly refuse to sign up to the underlying bargain. Hizbollah rejects the direct Israel-Lebanon negotiations outright, insisting that Lebanon entrust Iran, the group’s patron, with securing a full Israeli withdrawal as part of Tehran’s negotiations with Washington. 56 “ Hezbollah insists on linking Lebanon to Iran-U.S. negotiations ”, Asharq al-Awsat , 13 July 2026. Though Israel has participated in the trilateral talks with Lebanon and the U.S., it refuses to accept another arrangement like Resolution 1701, under which its troops withdrew from Lebanon after the 2006 war while Hizbollah remained under arms. Debates about a future international presence will also be shaped by U.S. and Israeli scepticism. Israel has long questioned the value of UNIFIL in helping Lebanon constrain Hizbollah, and it has shown little appetite for a replacement that might obstruct its own military operations. The U.S. does not oppose an international mission per se, but it is wary of replicating a UNIFIL model that it deems ineffective. 57 Crisis Group interviews, diplomats and UN officials, Beirut, July 2026. The U.S. and its Israeli partners have long argued that UNIFIL has failed to deter Hizbollah military operations south of the Litani River (even if it has no mandate to confront the militant group by force) and is too expensive. For background, see David Wood, “ Helping UNIFIL Restore Stability in Southern Lebanon ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 August 2025. Washington has sidelined the monitoring mechanism attached to the November 2024 ceasefire, in which UNIFIL and France (the Council’s penholder on Lebanon) were represented. Instead, an annex of the June framework agreement provides for a U.S.-headed “military coordination group”, through which Israel and Lebanon will manage tasks that UNIFIL or a successor force might have helped tackle, including “deconfliction, verification and overall implementation”. 58 The parties did not officially release this annex to the framework agreement, but they have not challenged the authenticity of a text leaked to the media in late June. “ The Lebanon-Israel ‘security’ annex agreement revealed ”, L’Orient Today , 29 June 2026. Other Council members and Lebanon strongly favour retaining an international presence, having reluctantly agreed to UNIFIL’s termination at the end of 2026 to avoid a U.S. veto that would have abruptly ended the mission in August 2025. 59 “ UN Interim Force in Lebanon: Vote on Final Mandate Renewal and Drawdown* ”, Security Council Report, 28 August 2025; Jamie Prentis, “ Lebanese MPs urge UN to extend peacekeeping mission ”, The National , 24 July 2026. The framework agreement does not mention the UN or Security Council resolution 1701. The annex, however, proposes a future role for a “mutually agreed-upon third-party entity” to verify that non-state armed groups have been cleared from each “pilot zone”. 60 “ The Lebanon-Israel ‘security’ annex agreement revealed ”, op. cit. To date, Israeli, Lebanese and U.S. negotiators have struggled to flesh out what such verification would entail, making it difficult for interested nations to commit troops to a mission that might prove dangerous. Yet even if the framework agreement eventually falls by the wayside, any other attempt to reach a deal that would link Israel’s withdrawal from southern Lebanon and cessation of airstrikes with an end to Hizbollah attacks on Israel and disarmament of the group would in all likelihood hinge on some sort of third-party verification. International partners have begun debating options for a new multinational presence. In June, the Secretary-General proposed a follow-up UN mission involving both armed and unarmed troops. 61 The report, mandated by the Security Council in Resolution 2790, proposed three different deployment sizes: the largest option would entail 5,525 uniformed personnel, the middle one 3,370 and the lightest footprint approximately 1,980. See “ Letter dated 1 June 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, UNSC S/2026/453, 1 June 2026. France and Italy have also announced plans to create a new multinational coalition in southern Lebanon as a successor to UNIFIL. 62 “ Lebanon president welcomes French, Italian efforts to form coalition to succeed UNIFIL ”, Arab News , 26 June 2026. In parallel, the European Union is weighing a separate mission comprising civilian and military personnel to advise and possibly train Lebanese forces – outside southern Lebanon – in addition to the €180 million it has already committed to support the Lebanese army. 63 Louay Faour, “ European powers seek greater role in south Lebanon’s post-war security architecture ”, The New Arab , 12 July 2026; Lili Bayer, “ EU diplomatic service proposes mission to train Lebanese forces, documents show ”, Reuters, 24 June 2026;“ European Peace Facility: Council adopts EUR 100 million assistance measure in support of the Lebanese Armed Forces ”, press release, Council of the EU, 4 June 2026. Any new multinational mission would have no choice but to work alongside the Lebanese-Israeli-U.S. security arrangement, even if that is not fully defined. States wishing to participate in a mission would almost certainly demand Security Council authorisation prior to sending troops to southern Lebanon so as to guarantee their legal and political protection. Given U.S. veto power, Washington’s support on the Council remains indispensable, meaning that UN members cannot circumvent the trilateral mechanism championed by the Trump administration. Between now and the end of December, diplomats should monitor the evolution of security arrangements on the ground in southern Lebanon, while seeking to work out with Washington what kind of international deployment, if any, would be beneficial to Lebanon and its stability. It is unlikely that any security arrangement, whether the June framework agreement and/or some future deal, will either fully disarm Hizbollah or completely dissuade Israel from conducting military operations in Lebanon. But withdrawing UNIFIL, with no immediate successor in place, could leave a vacuum that makes an already tense situation even more volatile. By inheriting UNIFIL’s most valuable functions – in particular, monitoring and on-the-ground deconfliction – a new multinational mission could set up a guardrail against fresh escalation. Ideally, that force would eventually assume other roles in bolstering a sustainable security arrangement for southern Lebanon that becomes durable enough to stand on its own feet. 2. Adapting the UN’s political strategy for Sudan The UN continues to be on the margins of diplomacy aimed at halting Sudan’s devastating civil war. Secretary-General Guterres’ appointment of Pekka Haavisto as the new UN envoy in February has offered the organisation an opportunity to refresh its approach. Ramtane Lamamra – the UN’s previous diplomatic lead – struggled to find a bridge between the main warring parties, the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), or to coordinate the array of mediators working to resolve the conflict. The UN has had varying degrees of success in securing local deals over aid access, and it continues to prepare for a possible role in overseeing aspects of a mooted ceasefire. 64 See the Sudan entry in Crisis Group Briefing, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2025-2026 , op. cit. It is hard to see the UN leading efforts to stop the war, given the number of powerful foreign states backing the belligerents, but it should use the coming months to support other diplomatic tracks and raise global awareness of the urgent need to end the fighting. 65 “ Sudan: Closed Consultations ”, Security Council Report, 17 April 2026. Nearly eighteen months ago, UN officials acknowledged that Sudan’s plight had become the world’s largest humanitarian catastrophe. 66 “ UN Sudan Annual Results Report 2024 ”, UN Sudan, 4 June 2025. Conditions have only deteriorated since then. An independent UN panel determined that mass killings, rapes and other atrocities committed by the RSF in October 2025 in El Fasher, Darfur – the city that hosted the headquarters of the former UN peacekeeping operation UNAMID – were “indicators of a genocidal path”. 67 “ Sudan: Hallmarks of Genocide in El Fasher - Report of the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan ”, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), UN Doc A/HRC/61/77, 19 February 2026. Diplomats and UN officials alike are sounding the alarm about similar risks in El-Obeid, North Kordofan. 68 “ Sudan: Imminent offensive on El Obeid must be halted – Türk warns of catastrophic impact on civilians ”, press release, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, 18 June 2026; “ Joint Statement of G7 Foreign Ministers on El Obeid, Sudan ”, U.S. Department of State, July 2026; “ Security Council Press Statement on Sudan (SC/16392) ”, UN Security Council, 20 June 2026. The two warring sides and their outside backers still believe there is more to gain from fighting than from negotiations. As matters stand, the country is in effect partitioned between the army and the RSF. 69 Crisis Group Africa Report N°211, Divided Sudan, Elusive Peace , 13 April 2026. To date, political negotiations have yielded few results. Much of the diplomatic focus has fallen on the Quad, a platform involving the U.S. and the three Arab powers with the most sway over the conflict parties – Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Its September 2025 roadmap, however, has won over neither belligerent, while Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, at loggerheads in conflict settings from Libya to Yemen, are doubling down on backing the army and RSF, respectively, stymying agreement within the Quad about what to do. 70 “ Joint Statement on Restoring Peace and Security in Sudan ”, U.S. Department of State, 12 September 2025; Comfort Ero and Alan Boswell, “ Latest Sudan Conference Shows Diplomacy is Backsliding ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 17 April 2026. In parallel, the UN is working alongside the African Union (AU), the EU, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), a Horn of Africa body, and the Arab League to support Sudanese-led civilian political dialogues as part of a nascent diplomatic track called the Quintet; these mediators convened a meeting in Berlin in April and another in Addis Ababa two months later. 71 “ Sudan: Quintet Joint Statement on de-escalation of the conflict in Sudan ”, European External Action Service, 11 February 2026; “ Quintet Statement on Ongoing Consultations with Sudanese Political Actors ”, African Union, 6 June 2026. Sudanese participants cannot agree on how to move forward with the talks, however. Having completed an initial tour of Sudan and the region, Haavisto can begin revising the UN’s diplomatic strategy. 72 “ Pekka Haavisto (Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Sudan) on the situation in the country – Press Conference ”, Office of the UN Spokesperson, 25 June 2026. He will need to reassure all parties that the UN will be an independent, impartial counterpart, even though the army-led government is the legally recognised one in New York. Haavisto needs to build rapport with others across Sudan’s fragmented political spectrum, including armed, political and civil players that are enlisted in the war, on one side or the other, or are non-aligned, as well as the various African, Arab and other countries directly involved in the conflict in one way or another. He will also need to reach out to the RSF, even if its deeds have earned it widespread and deserved condemnation. Lamamra struggled to maintain this balance, with critics seeing him as weighting his engagements too heavily toward the army-led authorities and its allies. 73 Crisis Group interviews, opposition political figures; RSF officials and allies, October-November 2025. Haavisto now has a chance for a reset. Haavisto should also strengthen the UN’s contributions within the Quintet. He could begin by stepping up outreach to various civilian groups between official Quintet meetings, with a view to mending fences between them. He could also help institute more consistent interactions between the Quintet and the army-led government, which has so far proven reluctant to get involved with a political process that is independent of its authority and takes place outside the country. 74 “ Quintet Statement Ahead of Visit to Khartoum, the Republic of Sudan, 8-10 September ”, Delegation of the European Union to the African Union, 8 September 2026. The army is instead pursuing its own “national dialogue” inside Sudan, which few of its political or armed opponents look likely to join. Behind the scenes, the UN should ... search for opportunities to bolster and connect the two diplomatic coalitions driving peace efforts [in Sudan]. Behind the scenes, the UN should also search for opportunities to bolster and connect the two diplomatic coalitions driving peace efforts, neither of which appears to have momentum at present. One way forward would be for Haavisto to work closely with counterparts to quietly float proposals for how Sudan could be governed whenever the main belligerents and their outside patrons summon the political will to seek an end to the war. Haavisto could help communicate these proposals to Quad and Quintet members, the two warring parties, and Sudan’s other main political movements and figures. Though it is hard to imagine a breakthrough any time soon given the entrenched positions on both sides, the UN should separately continue planning for a possible role in backing humanitarian access and ceasefire arrangements between the army and RSF should regional support for peace efforts eventually rise. 75 The UN is not formal member of the Quad, but it has worked informally with the U.S. to scope out technicalities of a monitoring mechanism for the prospective humanitarian truce that was outlined in the Quad’s September 2025 roadmap. The next Secretary-General should make this task a priority – including by paying a solidarity visit to refugee camps in countries neighbouring Sudan – and also warn of the mounting risks to states in the Horn and Red Sea regions should the conflict fester. 76 Alan Boswell, “ As the Horn of Africa Nears Boiling Point, Time for Urgent Diplomacy ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 17 July 2026. The UN’s new leader should ensure that Haavisto and other UN envoys covering the Horn, central Africa and the Middle East remain in close contact in the hope of identifying opportunities to break the diplomatic deadlock among states in these areas. 3. Encouraging a role for the General Assembly in Gaza’s ceasefire Having repeatedly called for a ceasefire to halt Israel’s campaign against Hamas in Gaza from 2023-2025, the General Assembly has devoted little energy to discussing whether the mechanisms created to uphold it are working. The Security Council’s November 2025 endorsement of the Trump administration’s ceasefire plan in Resolution 2803 – including its highly unusual authorisation of a Trump-chaired Board of Peace to serve as Gaza’s transitional administration – has erected a de-facto firewall between the UN and the diplomatic apparatus overseeing the Palestinian enclave’s future, at least until the Board’s UN mandate expires at the end of 2027. 77 “Resolution 2803”, op. cit. With Gaza’s reconstruction at a virtual standstill and Israel tightening its grip on the territory, UN member states risk sitting idle as the U.S.-dominated Board veers further off course. 78 Crisis Group Middle East Report N°257, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , 24 August 2026. The Board’s backtracking on the terms of its own fifteen-point roadmap – which features a scheme for decommissioning Hamas’s weapons agreed to by Palestinian factions but opposed by Israel – is just one of many troubling developments. The Security Council is, unfortunately, unlikely to consider corrective action until the Board mandate’s 2027 sunset. In the interim, member states should at a minimum use the General Assembly to assess the Board’s performance and to catalyse diplomatic pressure for putting Gaza on track toward recovery and Palestinian statehood. The General Assembly was the hub of UN diplomatic activity on Gaza throughout the war, as both President Joe Biden and President Trump blocked the Security Council from taking meaningful action. UN members convened the Assembly’s Emergency Special Session on the Occupied Palestinian Territories (its dedicated format for discussing the broader conflict) on eight separate occasions, and they debated five failed Security Council resolutions. 79 The General Assembly debated the nine vetoed resolutions under a Liechtenstein-led veto initiative, established by the General Assembly in April 2022. For full list of General Assembly meetings convened under the veto initiative, see “ Living with the Veto ”, Security Council Report, 23 March 2026, p. 8. Member states adopted five major General Assembly decisions on various aspects of the conflict, including the New York Declaration of September 2025, which bolstered recognition of Palestinian statehood. 80 “ Admission of new Members to the United Nations ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/23, 10 May 2024; Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/24, 19 September 2024; “ Support for the mandate of the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/25, 16 December 2024; “ Protection of civilians and upholding legal and humanitarian obligations ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/27, 13 June 2025; “ Endorsement of the New York Declaration on the Peaceful Settlement of the Question of Palestine and the Implementation of the Two-State Solution ”, UNGA A/80/L.1/Rev.1, 10 September 2025. Though these measures had limited impact on the ground, they signalled growing international opposition to the war’s trajectory. The Security Council’s endorsement of Trump’s ceasefire plan upended these dynamics. By agreeing to the U.S.-drafted resolution (unenthusiastically supported by regional mediators and the State of Palestine), they in effect outsourced all responsibility for Gaza’s recovery and governance to the Board of Peace. 81 In Resolution 2803, the Security Council authorises the Board of Peace to set up a transitional administration (supervising a Palestinian technocratic committee, as well as matters including reconstruction of Gaza, public services, humanitarian assistance, movement of persons in and out of the strip and the envisioned International Stabilisation Force. “Resolution 2803”, op. cit.; Forti, Gowan and Rodenbeck, “What to Look for as the Gaza Peace Plan Comes to the UN Security Council”, op. cit. Since then, the UN has been further isolated from diplomacy on Gaza. The Board’s High Representative Nickolay Mladenov (a former UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process) has briefed the Council and submitted a report (as required by Resolution 2803), but the General Assembly has discussed the situation only once – indirectly – since November 2025. No member state has asked to reconvene the Emergency Special Session despite worsening conditions under the tenuous truce. 83 General Assembly Annual Event of the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People Commemorating the Nakba, 15 May 2026. The inattention seems particularly negligent given that Gaza’s circumstances are diverging from not only Resolution 2803, but also the array of General Assembly resolutions and international legal orders about Palestine. 84 Crisis Group Report, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , op. cit. The lack of tangible progress in nearly a year after reaching a purported ceasefire makes international actors complicit in a brutal status quo: Gaza’s people are in effect hostage to diplomatic forces outside their control. Unless something changes, they will remain under siege, subject to bombardment and denied a future until the Board of Peace decides that Hamas has met Israel’s demands. Washington would likely veto any Security Council action perceived to criticise Israel – which receives unconditional backing from the U.S. at the UN – or to cast doubt on the legitimacy and efficacy of Trump’s peace efforts. But that ought not to be a justification for inaction in the General Assembly or elsewhere.
